title: Threads & Scheduling
summary: What threads are and how to use them, then how the OS decides who runs: classic algorithms, priorities and MLFQ, Linux's CFS and EEVDF, real-time classes, and scheduling across many cores and inside containers.

lessons.title: What threads share and keep private
lessons.summary: Threads have their own execution state while sharing the process address space and resources.
lessons.body:
A **process** is a running program with its own address space, open files and other resources. A **thread** is a single sequence of execution *inside* a process: its own program counter, registers and stack, running through the process's code.

Every process starts with one thread. A **multithreaded** process has several, all running the same program and all seeing the same memory.

A useful picture: the process is a kitchen (ingredients, utensils, ovens), and threads are cooks. Adding cooks lets several dishes progress at once, but they share the fridge, so they can get in each other's way.
## Why bother with threads?

You could get concurrency from several processes instead. Threads exist because they make some things much easier or cheaper:

- **Parallelism.** A machine with 16 cores can run 16 threads of one program at the same instant. A single application thread cannot itself execute on several cores simultaneously; libraries or the kernel may do work on its behalf.
- **Overlapping waiting with work.** While one thread blocks on a disk read or network reply, another can keep computing or serve another user.
- **Responsiveness.** A GUI keeps a thread free to handle input while a worker thread does the slow job.
- **Cheap sharing.** Threads communicate by reading and writing the same memory. Processes need pipes, sockets or explicitly shared memory.
- **Cheaper to create and switch.** A new thread does not need a new address space. Sharing an address space can avoid changing memory maps and preserve useful translations. Cache residency and measured switch cost still depend on hardware and workload.

The price of cheap sharing is that **nothing stops two threads touching the same data at the same time**. That is the subject of the next module (synchronisation). For now, just remember that shared data needs a lock or similar protection.
## Shared versus private state

This table is the heart of the lesson. If you know which column something is in, you can predict most multithreading bugs.

| Shared by all threads | Private to each thread |
|---|---|
| Code (text segment) | Program counter |
| Global and static variables | Registers |
| Heap (`malloc`, Python objects) | Stack (locals, return addresses) |
| Open file descriptors | Thread ID |
| Current directory, user ID | Signal mask |
| Signal handlers, PID | Scheduling priority, `errno`, thread-local storage |

In memory it looks like this. Each thread gets its own stack somewhere in the shared address space:

```
high  +------------------------+
      | stack: main thread     |
      +------------------------+
      | stack: thread 2        |
      +------------------------+
      | stack: thread 3        |
      +------------------------+
      |          ...           |
      | heap (shared)          |
      +------------------------+
      | globals / static       |
      +------------------------+
low   | code                   |
      +------------------------+
```

Note that "private" stacks are private by convention, not by hardware. All threads share one address space, so a thread that is handed a pointer to another thread's local variable can read and corrupt it. Nothing is truly walled off.

A small C example makes the split concrete:

```c
#include <pthread.h>
#include <stdio.h>

int hits = 0;      /* global: shared */

void *work(void *arg) {
    int mine = 0;  /* on this stack */
    mine++;
    /* Unsafe update of a shared counter. */
    hits++;        /* C data race */
    printf("mine=%d\n", mine);
    return NULL;
}
```

Each call has its own `mine`, but the unsynchronised accesses to shared `hits` create a C data race and therefore undefined behaviour: this program has no guaranteed output. The read/add/write lost-update model illustrates one possible failure, not the full language semantics. Use an atomic counter or lock before relying on the output. The question uses C11 atomic_fetch_add for the shared counter: that indivisible update removes this race, while each call still has its own local mine value. Three completed calls then each print mine=1 and leave the atomic counter at 3.

> [!warning] One thread's crash is everyone's crash
> Threads share fate. A signal with a terminating disposition (such as ordinary default-action SIGSEGV), or a call to exit(), terminates the whole process. Not every uncaught signal has a terminating default action. Processes isolate failures; threads do not.

## Key takeaways
- Threads have their own execution state while sharing the process address space and resources.
- A pointer can expose one thread’s stack to another; “private stack” is not a memory-protection boundary.
- A C data race makes the program undefined; an atomic increment or lock is needed for a reliable shared counter.

## Further reading
- [Concurrency: An Introduction — OSTEP](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-intro.pdf)
- [pthreads(7) — Linux manual page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/pthreads.7.html)
- [clone(2) — Linux manual page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/clone.2.html)
- [Native POSIX Thread Library — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_POSIX_Thread_Library)
- [Green thread — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_thread)
- [JEP 444: Virtual Threads — OpenJDK](https://openjdk.org/jeps/444)

questions.prompt: Which of these does each thread in a process get **its own copy** of?

options.text: The heap
options.explanation: The heap is shared: memory one thread allocates with `malloc` (or any Python object it creates) is visible to every thread that has a pointer to it.

options.text: Global variables
options.explanation: Globals live in the process's data segment, which all threads share. That is exactly why unprotected globals cause races.

options.text: The table of open file descriptors
options.explanation: File descriptors belong to the process. If one thread opens a file, another thread can read from that descriptor, and closing it closes it for all.

options.text: The stack
options.explanation: Correct. Each thread has its own stack holding its local variables and return addresses, because each thread is at a different point in its own chain of function calls.

questions.prompt: Select **all** of the following that are shared by every thread of a single process.

options.text: Objects allocated on the heap
options.explanation: Correct. There is one heap per process; any thread holding a pointer or reference can use the object.

options.text: Open file descriptors
options.explanation: Correct. The file descriptor table belongs to the process (on Linux, threads are created with `CLONE_FILES`).

options.text: The program counter
options.explanation: Wrong: each thread is at its own point in the code, so each has its own program counter. Sharing it would mean they were one thread.

options.text: Global variables
options.explanation: Correct. Globals live in the shared data segment, which is why they need protection when several threads write them.

options.text: The CPU registers
options.explanation: Wrong: registers are part of each thread's private execution context; the kernel saves and restores them on every switch.

questions.workedExample:
Sort each item into "process resource" or "execution context":

| Item | Belongs to |
|---|---|
| Heap | Process (shared) |
| File descriptors | Process (shared) |
| Globals | Process (shared) |
| Program counter | Thread (private) |
| Registers | Thread (private) |

The execution context (PC, registers, stack) is what makes a thread a thread. Everything else is shared.

options.text: `mine=1`, `mine=2`, `mine=3` in some order
options.explanation: This would be true only if `mine` were shared. It is a local variable, so each thread has its own copy on its own stack.

options.text: `mine=1` three times
options.explanation: Correct. `mine` lives on each thread's private stack, starts at 0 and is incremented once, so every thread prints 1. It is `hits` that is shared.

options.text: `mine=3` three times
options.explanation: That assumes all three increments land on the same variable before anyone prints. Locals are per thread, so no thread ever sees another's increment.

options.text: It is unpredictable because of a data race on `mine`
options.explanation: There is no race on `mine`, and the shared `hits` update uses an atomic operation. Each call prints its own `mine` value.

questions.workedExample: Each call has its own automatic `mine` variable, increments it from 0 to 1 and prints `mine=1`. The shared `hits` counter is now atomic, so three completed calls increment it to 3 without a data race. The original non-atomic `hits++` would make the entire C program undefined, even though `mine` itself was not shared.

questions.prompt: Select **all** correct reasons why switching between two threads of the **same** process is usually cheaper than switching between two different processes.

options.text: The page tables stay the same, so there is no address-space switch
options.explanation: Correct. Both threads use the same address space, so the kernel doesn't load a new page-table root.

options.text: Cached address translations in the TLB stay valid
options.explanation: Correct. Because the address space doesn't change, the TLB entries still apply, avoiding a burst of TLB misses afterwards.

options.text: Threads don't have registers that need saving
options.explanation: Wrong: every thread has its own registers and the kernel must save and restore them on each switch, just as for processes.

options.text: The kernel is not involved in switching between kernel threads
options.explanation: Wrong: kernel threads are scheduled by the kernel, so a switch still involves entering the kernel. Only user-level threads avoid it.

options.text: The CPU caches are more likely to hold useful data
options.explanation: Correct. The threads share code and often data, so the incoming thread may find some of its working set already in cache.

questions.workedExample: Both cases save/restore thread state. Sharing an address space can avoid changing memory maps, and shared code/data can preserve useful locality. Translation validity is not guaranteed cache residency; PCID can preserve process translations too. These are possible savings, not a universal ordering of measured switch latency.

questions.prompt: A worker in a 50-thread process incurs a memory fault that generates SIGSEGV, with its default terminating disposition unchanged. What happens?

options.text: The whole process, including all 50 threads, is killed
options.explanation: Correct. Threads share one address space and one set of signal dispositions, so a fatal signal in any thread terminates the entire process.

options.text: Only that worker thread dies; the other 49 keep serving
options.explanation: That is the isolation processes give you, not threads. A SIGSEGV's default action terminates the whole process.

options.text: The thread is restarted automatically by the threads library
options.explanation: pthreads has no supervisor that restarts crashed threads. The default action for SIGSEGV kills the process.

options.text: Nothing, because each thread has its own private memory
options.explanation: Threads share memory; only their stacks are separate, and even those aren't protected. A NULL dereference raises SIGSEGV for the process.

questions.workedExample: SIGSEGV with its ordinary default action terminates the process, ending all 50 threads. Separate processes provide a memory-isolation boundary, but shared resources and recovery policy can still couple failures; a worker crash does not guarantee that every other service process continues uninterrupted.

lessons.title: Mapping user threads onto kernel tasks
lessons.summary: N:1 cannot execute user threads on several cores and a blocking syscall can stop the whole runtime.
lessons.body:
## Kernel threads and user threads

There are two places a thread can be implemented.

**Kernel threads** are known to the OS. The kernel schedules each one independently, so they can run on different cores, and one blocking in a system call does not stop the others.

**User threads** (also called user-level or green threads) are managed by a library or language runtime inside the process. The kernel sees only the process (or a few kernel threads). The runtime switches between user threads itself, by saving and restoring registers, without a system call.

| | Kernel threads | User threads |
|---|---|---|
| Create / switch | OS-managed work | Runtime-managed work |
| Use many cores | Yes | Only via kernel threads |
| Blocking syscall | Blocks one thread | May block all |
| Scheduling | OS policy | Runtime's policy |
## Threading models: 1:1, N:1 and M:N

The models describe how user-visible threads map onto kernel threads.

```
1:1         N:1          M:N
U U U       U U U U      U U U U U
| | |        \ | | /      \ |/ \|/
K K K          K           K    K
```
## 1:1 (one-to-one)

Each thread you create is a kernel thread. Simple, uses all cores, and blocking calls behave as expected. The costs are a system call per creation and a kernel-sized footprint per thread.

**Linux uses 1:1.** Since glibc 2.3.2 and Linux 2.6 (around 2003), pthreads are provided by **NPTL** (Native POSIX Thread Library), and every `pthread_create` makes a kernel task. Windows and modern macOS are also 1:1.
## N:1 (many-to-one)

All user threads are multiplexed onto one kernel thread. Switching is very fast, but:

- the process can never use more than one core;
- if any user thread makes a blocking system call (say a `read` on a socket), the single kernel thread blocks and every user thread stops.

Early Java on Solaris ("green threads") worked this way. The model has largely died out for general-purpose threads.
## M:N (many-to-many)

M user threads run on N kernel threads, with N usually around the number of cores. It promises the best of both: cheap threads and real parallelism. It is also the hardest to build, because two schedulers (the runtime's and the kernel's) must cooperate, and blocking calls need special handling.

Solaris used M:N before Solaris 9 and then switched to 1:1. Linux had a competing M:N project (NGPT) that lost to NPTL. For OS-level threads, 1:1 won because the kernel made kernel threads cheap enough.
## How Linux actually does it

To the Linux kernel there is no separate "thread" object. Both processes and threads are **tasks** (`struct task_struct`), created by the `clone()` system call. The flags decide what is shared:

```
fork():   private address space
          (memory copied on write)

thread:   clone(CLONE_VM | CLONE_FS |
                CLONE_FILES |
                CLONE_SIGHAND |
                CLONE_THREAD | ...)
```

`CLONE_VM` shares the address space, `CLONE_FILES` shares the file descriptor table and `CLONE_THREAD` puts the new task in the same **thread group**. What user space calls the PID is really the thread group ID (TGID). Each thread has its own ID, which `gettid()` returns.

You can see this from the shell:

```
$ ps -eLf | head -3     # -L shows threads
$ ls /proc/1234/task/   # one dir per thread
```

Because each thread is a separate task, the Linux scheduler schedules threads, not processes. A process with 8 runnable threads competes as 8 tasks (unless cgroups group them, as later lessons show).

## Key takeaways
- N:1 cannot execute user threads on several cores and a blocking syscall can stop the whole runtime.
- Linux pthreads use 1:1 mappings; runtimes can instead multiplex user threads over kernel threads.
- Linux getpid identifies the thread group, while gettid identifies the calling kernel task.

## Further reading
- [Concurrency: An Introduction — OSTEP](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-intro.pdf)
- [pthreads(7) — Linux manual page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/pthreads.7.html)
- [clone(2) — Linux manual page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/clone.2.html)
- [Native POSIX Thread Library — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_POSIX_Thread_Library)
- [Green thread — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_thread)
- [JEP 444: Virtual Threads — OpenJDK](https://openjdk.org/jeps/444)

questions.prompt: A runtime uses the **N:1** model: 20 user-level threads multiplexed onto one kernel thread. One user thread calls a blocking `read()` on a socket that has no data yet. What happens?

options.text: Only that user thread waits; the runtime switches to another user thread
options.explanation: That is how M:N runtimes such as Go behave, because they use non-blocking I/O or extra kernel threads. In plain N:1, the kernel only sees one thread, and it is now blocked.

options.text: The kernel schedules another of the 20 user threads instead
options.explanation: The kernel doesn't know the 20 user threads exist. It sees a single kernel thread, which is asleep in `read()`.

options.text: All 20 user threads stop until the read returns
options.explanation: Correct. The one kernel thread is blocked inside the kernel, so the runtime's scheduler never gets to run, and no user thread can make progress.

options.text: The read fails immediately with EAGAIN
options.explanation: Only a socket set to non-blocking mode returns EAGAIN. The question says a blocking `read()`.

questions.workedExample:
1. In N:1, the kernel sees **one** schedulable entity.
2. A blocking `read()` with no data puts that kernel thread to sleep inside the kernel.
3. The user-level scheduler is just code running on that same kernel thread, so it can't run either.
4. All 20 user threads are stuck until data arrives.

This is the classic weakness of N:1, and why M:N runtimes wrap blocking calls (non-blocking sockets plus `epoll`, or handing off to another kernel thread).

questions.prompt: On Linux, process 1234 has 5 threads. The **main** thread calls `getpid()` and `gettid()`, and another thread calls `getpid()`. What values do they see?

options.text: Main: 1234 and 1234. Other thread: 1234
options.explanation: Correct. The PID is really the thread group ID, which equals the TID of the first (main) thread. Every thread in the group gets 1234 from `getpid()`; other threads have their own TIDs.

options.text: Main: 1234 and 0. Other thread: 1235
options.explanation: TIDs are never 0, and `getpid()` returns the thread group ID for every thread, not a per-thread number.

options.text: Main: 1234 and 1. Other thread: 1234
options.explanation: Thread IDs are not numbered from 1 within a process; they come from the same system-wide ID space as PIDs.

options.text: Main: 1234 and 1234. Other thread: a different number
options.explanation: `getpid()` returns the same thread group ID in every thread. Only `gettid()` differs between threads.

questions.workedExample:
1. In Linux every thread is a task with its own ID (the TID).
2. Threads of one process form a **thread group**; the group's ID (TGID) is what user space calls the PID.
3. The TGID is the TID of the first task in the group, the main thread. So in the main thread `getpid() == gettid() == 1234`.
4. Another thread has its own TID (say 1240), but `getpid()` still returns 1234.

You can see the TIDs with `ls /proc/1234/task/`.

questions.prompt: A CPU-bound program creates 32 user-level threads with an **N:1** threads library and runs on an 8-core machine. At best, how much faster is it than running the same work in a single thread?

options.text: 8 times faster
options.explanation: That would need 8 kernel threads on 8 cores. N:1 maps everything onto a single kernel thread, which can be on only one core at a time.

options.text: 32 times faster
options.explanation: You can't exceed the number of cores even with 1:1, and here there is only one kernel thread.

options.text: 4 times faster, because of hyper-threading
options.explanation: Hyper-threading helps only when there are several kernel threads to place on the logical CPUs; with N:1 there is just one.

options.text: About the same speed, or slightly slower
options.explanation: Correct. All user threads share one kernel thread, so only one core is ever used. The extra switching makes it, if anything, slightly slower.

questions.workedExample:
1. Parallelism requires several **kernel** threads, because the kernel is what places threads on cores.
2. N:1 gives the kernel exactly one thread to schedule.
3. One kernel thread can run on one core at a time, so the maximum speedup over a single thread is 1×.
4. User-level switches cost a little, so it may even be slightly slower.

N:1 is useful for structuring concurrent code (and for very cheap switches) but not for using multiple cores.

lessons.title: Lightweight runtimes and thread resource limits
lessons.summary: Goroutines and virtual threads share carrier threads; their counts do not determine an exact OS-thread count.
lessons.body:
## Green threads return: goroutines and virtual threads

M:N came back, not in the OS but in language runtimes, where the runtime controls the whole stack and can avoid the classic pitfalls.

**Go's goroutines** are the best-known example:

- A goroutine starts with a small stack that grows as needed. The Go 1.25 source sets the minimum Go stack to 2048 bytes; platform overhead and allocation rounding can raise the actual initial allocation. Large goroutine counts remain limited by memory and workload.
- The runtime runs them on a small set of OS threads. `GOMAXPROCS` limits simultaneous Go execution. Go 1.25 introduced defaults that also consider container CPU limits; explicit settings and compatibility controls can override that policy.
- When a goroutine does network I/O, the runtime parks it and uses non-blocking sockets plus `epoll` behind the scenes, so the OS thread is free for other goroutines. For genuinely blocking system calls, the runtime hands the thread's work to another thread.
- Since Go 1.14, the runtime can **preempt** a goroutine stuck in a tight loop, improving responsiveness for ordinary tight loops; this is not an unconditional scheduling-latency guarantee.

**Java virtual threads** (final in JDK 21) do the same for Java: lightweight threads mounted on carrier OS threads; achievable counts and carrier behavior depend on memory, runtime version and workload. Erlang's lightweight processes are an older example of the same idea.

> [!tip] Why not just make OS threads cheaper?
> An OS thread needs a kernel stack, a `task_struct` and a user stack. For Linux NPTL, a finite RLIMIT_STACK soft limit at program start determines the default new-thread stack size; 8 MiB is one common configuration, not a universal default. Reserving stack address space does not mean every page is resident in RAM. The feasible thread count depends on resource limits, stack configuration and workload. A goroutine's few KB scale much further.
## Pitfalls to remember

- **Shared by default.** Globals and heap objects are visible to every thread. Accidental sharing is the most common source of bugs.
- **More threads is not more speed.** For CPU-bound work, start from available logical CPUs and measure; SMT, quotas, memory bandwidth and serial work affect the useful concurrency.
- **`fork()` in a threaded program** copies only the calling thread. Any lock another thread held is copied in its locked state, with no thread left to unlock it. After `fork()` in a multithreaded process, call only async-signal-safe functions until `exec()`.
- **Thread IDs are not process IDs.** Tools like `top` (press `H`) or `htop` can show per-thread CPU use, which is often where the hot spot hides.

> [!note] Content gap: thread capacity and timing
> No reproducible benchmark supports universal thread creation/switch timings, maximum thread counts or a fixed Go OS-thread count. These figures are omitted; limits and costs depend on runtime, platform and workload.

## Key takeaways
- Goroutines and virtual threads share carrier threads; their counts do not determine an exact OS-thread count.
- Reserved stack address space differs from physical memory committed to touched pages.
- After fork in a multithreaded child, use only async-signal-safe operations until exec.

## Further reading
- [Concurrency: An Introduction — OSTEP](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-intro.pdf)
- [pthreads(7) — Linux manual page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/pthreads.7.html)
- [clone(2) — Linux manual page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/clone.2.html)
- [Native POSIX Thread Library — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_POSIX_Thread_Library)
- [Green thread — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_thread)
- [JEP 444: Virtual Threads — OpenJDK](https://openjdk.org/jeps/444)
- [Go 1.25 runtime stack implementation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/golang/go/go1.25.0/src/runtime/stack.go)
- [Container-aware GOMAXPROCS — Go team](https://go.dev/blog/container-aware-gomaxprocs)

questions.prompt: A 64-bit Linux service requests 10,000 threads, each with an explicitly configured 8 MiB user stack. It has 32 GiB of RAM. Which statement correctly distinguishes virtual reservations from physical memory?

options.text: It needs about 80 GB of RAM, so thread creation fails partway through
options.explanation: This confuses reserved virtual memory with physical memory. Stacks are mapped lazily; untouched pages use no RAM.

options.text: User stacks reserve about 78.125 GiB of address space; physical memory is demand-backed, but creation can still fail because of resource or commit limits
options.explanation: 10,000 × 8 MiB = 80,000 MiB = 78.125 GiB of virtual stack space, excluding guards and other mappings. Actual resident and kernel memory, commit policy and task limits determine feasibility.

options.text: All 10,000 threads share one 8 MB stack, so it uses only 8 MB
options.explanation: Each thread needs its own stack; sharing one would mean threads overwrite each other's local variables.

options.text: It is impossible: Linux allows at most 1,024 threads per process
options.explanation: There is no 1,024 limit. Limits come from settings such as `threads-max`, `pid_max`, `ulimit -u` and memory, and are typically far higher.

questions.workedExample:
Add up what is reserved and, separately, what might actually be touched:

```formula
M_res = N s_stack
M_res = 10000 × 8 MiB = 80000 MiB
M_res = (80000 / 1024) GiB = 78.125 GiB
M_used = N(s_user + s_kern)
M_used = 10000 × (20 KiB + 16 KiB)
M_used = 360000 KiB = 351.5625 MiB
where
M_res: the virtual address space reserved for user stacks
N: the number of threads, 10,000
s_stack: the configured user-stack size per thread, 8 MiB
M_used: a hypothetical amount of stack memory actually backed by RAM
s_user: an assumed 20 KiB of each user stack actually touched (an illustration, not a measurement)
s_kern: the kernel stack per thread, assumed 16 KiB
KiB: kibibyte, 1024 bytes
MiB: mebibyte, 1024 KiB (1,048,576 bytes)
GiB: gibibyte, 1024 MiB
In words: the reservations add up to far more than the 32 GiB of RAM, but RAM is only used for pages that are touched, which here is well under a gibibyte.
```

User-stack reservations total 78.125 GiB. The touched-stack subtotal is about 351.6 MiB; task metadata, guard pages, other mappings and other memory add costs. This does not establish that 10,000 creations succeed: check limits, commit policy and workload.

questions.prompt: Thread A calls `fork()` while thread B, in the same process, is inside a logging library's `log()` function holding the library's internal mutex. In the child, the single thread then calls `log()`. What is the risk?

options.text: None: the child gets fresh copies of all locks in the unlocked state
options.explanation: `fork()` copies memory as-is, so a lock that was held is copied in its held state. Nothing resets it.

options.text: The child deadlocks: it has a copy of the lock in its held state, but thread B was not copied, so nothing will ever release it
options.explanation: Correct. Only the calling thread exists in the child. The lock B held is still marked as held in the child's memory, and its owner is gone.

options.text: Thread B is copied too and finishes its `malloc`, releasing the lock
options.explanation: POSIX `fork()` duplicates only the calling thread. Thread B doesn't exist in the child.

options.text: The kernel detects the held lock and makes `fork()` fail
options.explanation: The kernel knows nothing about user-space locks like a library's mutex. `fork()` succeeds.

questions.workedExample:
1. `fork()` makes the child's memory a copy-on-write copy of the parent's, including the bytes that represent locks.
2. Only the thread that called `fork()` is duplicated.
3. At the instant of the fork, B held the logging mutex, so the copied mutex says "held".
4. In the child, `log()` tries to take the mutex and waits forever for an owner that doesn't exist.

(glibc protects its own `malloc` locks with special fork handling, but an arbitrary library's locks are not protected.) The rule: after `fork()` in a multithreaded program, call only async-signal-safe functions until `exec()`. Tools like `posix_spawn` avoid the problem.

questions.prompt: A Go service on Linux has 100,000 goroutines, each waiting on its own TCP connection most of the time. `GOMAXPROCS` is 4. Roughly how many OS threads does the process use?

options.text: About 100,000: one per goroutine
options.explanation: That would be a 1:1 model. Go multiplexes goroutines onto a small number of OS threads.

options.text: Exactly 1: Go runs all goroutines on a single thread
options.explanation: That would be N:1, and Go would be unable to use more than one core. Go runs goroutines on up to GOMAXPROCS threads at once.

options.text: GOMAXPROCS limits simultaneous Go execution to 4; network waiters are parked, but total OS-thread count is not determined by these facts
options.explanation: Go can multiplex many network waiters without one OS thread each. Runtime work, blocking calls, cgo and locked threads affect the total; four is an execution-parallelism limit.

options.text: About 25,000: one OS thread per 4 goroutines
options.explanation: There is no fixed ratio of goroutines to threads. Thread counts follow parallelism (GOMAXPROCS) plus threads stuck in blocking syscalls, not goroutine count.

questions.workedExample: Four Ps (the Go scheduler's logical processors, one per unit of GOMAXPROCS) limit simultaneous ordinary Go execution to four threads. Network goroutines can park on the Linux netpoller without dedicating one thread to each connection. The total thread count also depends on runtime, blocking calls and thread-affinity requirements, so it cannot be calculated from the supplied goroutine count and GOMAXPROCS alone.

lessons.title: Create threads and combine independent results
lessons.summary: Pass stable argument structures to pthread_create and check its returned error number.

questions.prompt: `pthread_create` fails because the system has hit its thread limit. How does it report the error?

options.text: It returns −1 and sets `errno` to `EAGAIN`
options.explanation: That is the convention for most system calls, but pthreads functions are different. Checking `errno` after a pthreads call is a common mistake.

options.text: It returns 0 and leaves the `pthread_t` set to NULL
options.explanation: 0 means success for pthreads functions; it would never signal failure that way.

options.text: It returns the error number (`EAGAIN`) directly
options.explanation: Correct. pthreads functions return 0 on success or an error number on failure, so you check the return value, e.g. with `strerror(rc)`.

options.text: It raises SIGSEGV in the calling thread
options.explanation: Resource exhaustion is reported through return values, not signals.

questions.workedExample:
1. Classic Unix system calls return −1 and put the reason in `errno`.
2. The pthreads functions were designed differently: they **return the error number** itself and return 0 on success.
3. For a thread limit (`RLIMIT_NPROC`, `threads-max`) or lack of memory, `pthread_create` returns `EAGAIN`.

So write:

This is a partial API pattern: replace the ellipsis with actual thread, attributes, start-function and argument values.

```c
int rc = pthread_create(...);
if (rc != 0)
    fprintf(stderr, "%s\n",
            strerror(rc));
```

options.text: There is a data race on `counts`, so the hardware serialises the updates
options.explanation: There's no race: each thread writes a different element. The slowdown is a cache effect, not a correctness issue.

options.text: Thread creation overhead dominates
options.explanation: Creation has overhead, but the question asks about repeated updates to neighbouring locations. Its absolute contribution requires measurement; it is not universally negligible.

options.text: The GIL prevents the threads running in parallel
options.explanation: This is C; there is no GIL. The threads do run in parallel, they just fight over one cache line.

options.text: False sharing: the counters occupy one cache line, so alternating writes from different cores can transfer its ownership
options.explanation: The aligned counters share a cache line. Ownership transfers can occur as cores alternate writes to different counters; not every increment necessarily transfers ownership.

questions.workedExample: With the explicit size and alignment assumptions, four counters occupy 32 bytes within one 64-byte line. Different cores repeatedly writing different elements can transfer ownership of that line: false sharing despite no same-element race. Accumulate locally then publish once, or use a suitably aligned per-counter stride of at least the measured cache-line size. No fixed slowdown or nanosecond transfer cost is implied.

lessons.title: Join, detach and preserve argument lifetimes
lessons.summary: Join or detach every successfully created joinable thread.
lessons.body:
## Join, detach, or leak

A finished joinable thread retains resources and a result for a later join. Its automatic local objects have already ended their lifetimes; retained or cached stack storage does not keep those objects alive:

- **Joinable** (the default): another thread must call `pthread_join`. If nobody ever does, the finished thread's resources are never freed. It is the thread equivalent of a zombie process.
- **Detached**: call `pthread_detach(tid)` (or create it with the `PTHREAD_CREATE_DETACHED` attribute). Its resources are freed as soon as it exits. You can no longer join it or get its result.

Use join when you need the result or need to know the work is done. Use detach for fire-and-forget background threads.

> [!warning] Returning from `main` kills every thread
> Returning from `main` calls `exit()`, which ends the whole process, including threads still running. Join your threads first, or end `main` with `pthread_exit(NULL)`, which ends only the main thread and lets the others carry on.
## The bugs everyone writes first

**Passing the loop variable's address:**

```c
/* Bug: every worker gets the same &i. */
for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++)
    pthread_create(&t[i], NULL, f, &i);
```

All four threads get a pointer to the *same* `i`. Concurrent unsynchronized reads and writes constitute a C data race (undefined behavior), and use after the loop can also exceed its lifetime. Duplicates or `4` are possible symptoms, not guaranteed outcomes. Give each thread its own argument: an array element, a `malloc`'d struct, or a platform-supported value-through-pointer convention (not a universally portable integer transport).

**Returning a pointer to a local.** A thread that returns `&result`, where `result` is a local variable, hands back a pointer to an object whose lifetime has ended, regardless of whether its stack storage is physically reclaimed yet. Return a heap pointer or write into memory the caller owns.

**Assuming an order.** Thread creation order says nothing about execution order. Threads started 1, 2, 3 may run, print and finish in any order.

## Key takeaways
- Join or detach every successfully created joinable thread.
- Returning from main ends the whole process; detaching does not extend its lifetime.
- Each worker needs a stable argument and a result object that outlives its use.

## Further reading
- [pthread_create(3) — Linux manual page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/pthread_create.3.html)
- [pthread_detach(3) — Linux manual page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/pthread_detach.3.html)
- [Interlude: Thread API — OSTEP](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-api.pdf)
- [concurrent.futures — Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/library/concurrent.futures.html)
- [Python support for free threading — Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/howto/free-threading-python.html)
- [PEP 703: Making the GIL optional in CPython](https://peps.python.org/pep-0703/)

questions.prompt: Select **all** true statements about joinable and detached POSIX threads.

options.text: A joinable thread that exits but is never joined keeps holding some resources
options.explanation: Correct. Some thread resources and the return value remain available for a later join. Automatic local objects have already ended their lifetimes; retained stack storage does not keep them alive.

options.text: A detached thread's resources are released automatically when it exits
options.explanation: Correct. That is the whole point of detaching: nobody needs to join it.

options.text: You can call `pthread_join` on a detached thread to get its return value
options.explanation: POSIX specifies undefined behaviour if the target is not a joinable thread. Linux may diagnose some invalid joins, but a program must not rely on joining a detached thread.

options.text: A detached thread keeps running after `main` returns
options.explanation: Wrong: detaching only affects cleanup. Returning from `main` still exits the process and kills every thread.

options.text: Calling `pthread_exit(NULL)` at the end of `main` lets other threads finish
options.explanation: Correct. It ends only the main thread; the process lives until the last thread exits.

questions.workedExample:
Separate two questions:

1. **Who frees a finished thread's resources?** Joinable: whoever joins it. Detached: the system, automatically. A joinable thread that's never joined leaks.
2. **When does the process end?** When any thread calls `exit()` (including returning from `main`), or when the last thread ends.

Detaching answers question 1 only. It doesn't protect a thread from the process exiting. `pthread_exit` in `main` is the way to let `main` finish without ending the process.

options.text: All threads receive the same changing i; concurrent unsynchronised reads and writes cause undefined behaviour
options.explanation: Duplicate or unexpected numbers can occur in ordinary runs, but the C language guarantees no output once the read/write data race occurs.

options.text: Only `0 1 2 3` in some order
options.explanation: That assumes each thread gets its own copy of `i`. They all receive the address of the same variable, which the loop keeps changing.

options.text: Always `4 4 4 4`
options.explanation: Possible if every thread starts late, but not guaranteed. Threads often start while the loop is still running, so they see 1, 2 or 3.

options.text: Nothing: it fails to compile because `&i` is an `int *`, not a `void *`
options.explanation: In C any object pointer converts implicitly to `void *`, so it compiles without complaint. The bug is in the logic, not the types.

questions.workedExample: The threads receive &i rather than copies of its value. The loop writes i while workers may read it without synchronisation, so there is a data race and undefined behaviour. Give each thread a distinct initialised element, pass its address, and keep that array alive until all joins complete.

options.text: It returns the address of a local object whose lifetime ends on return, so dereferencing it later is undefined behaviour
options.explanation: Correct. The automatic result object dies when compute returns. Retained or cached stack storage does not extend its lifetime; a later dereference can fail in arbitrary ways.

options.text: Nothing: `pthread_join` copies the returned value into `p`
options.explanation: `pthread_join` copies the *pointer*, not what it points to. The pointer refers to memory that is no longer valid.

options.text: `pthread_join` cannot return values; only `pthread_exit` can
options.explanation: Returning from the start function is equivalent to calling `pthread_exit` with that value, and `pthread_join` retrieves it.

options.text: It is a data race between `main` and the thread on `result`
options.explanation: `pthread_join` provides proper ordering: the thread is finished before `main` reads. The problem is that the memory is dead, not that it's raced.

Dereferencing its returned address is undefined behavior. Return heap storage with a clear owner, or write into a caller-owned result field. Integer-to-pointer conversions are not a universally portable result transport.

lessons.title: Reuse workers and estimate waiting-job waves
lessons.summary: A pool reuses a bounded number of workers rather than creating an unbounded thread per request.
lessons.body:
## Thread pools

Creating a thread involves allocation and runtime/OS work; no reproducible creation-time benchmark is supplied here. More importantly, a server that creates one thread per request without admission or concurrency limits has **no application-level bound**: a traffic spike can create thousands of threads until resource limits or failures intervene.

A bounded **thread pool** reuses workers and caps active jobs; its submission queue still needs an overload policy. A fixed set of worker threads pulls jobs from a shared queue:

```
 submit()     task queue      workers
 -------->  [t5][t4][t3]  -->  W1 (t1)
                          -->  W2 (t2)
                          -->  W3 (idle)
```

Threads are created once and reused, and the pool size caps concurrency. Examples include Java's `ExecutorService`, the worker pools in web servers, database connection handlers, and Python's `concurrent.futures`.

```python
from concurrent.futures import (
    ThreadPoolExecutor)
import time

def fetch(i):
    # Sleep releases the GIL while waiting.
    time.sleep(0.5)  # stands in for I/O
    return i * i

start = time.perf_counter()
pool = ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=10)
with pool as ex:
    # map yields results in input order.
    results = list(ex.map(fetch, range(20)))
took = time.perf_counter() - start

# Squares are fixed; duration varies.
print(results[:5], f"{took:.1f}s")
```

The values are `[0, 1, 4, 9, 16]`; the elapsed-time suffix is machine-dependent and should be near or above the ideal one-second schedule. When every job takes the same time, a pool works through them in "waves": each wave runs one job on every worker at once.

```formula
N_waves = ⌈N_jobs / N_workers⌉
T ≈ N_waves t_job
N_waves = ⌈20 / 10⌉ = 2
T ≈ 2 × 0.5 s = 1 s
where
N_waves: how many rounds of jobs the pool needs
N_jobs: the number of jobs submitted, 20 here
N_workers: the number of worker threads, 10 here (max_workers)
⌈x⌉: ceiling: round x up to the next whole number, because a part-filled last wave still takes a whole job's time
T: the total elapsed time, in seconds (s)
t_job: how long one job takes, 0.5 s here
≈: approximately equal to (ignores start-up and switching overhead)
s: seconds
In words: divide the jobs between the workers, round up to whole waves, and each wave takes as long as one job.
```

So twenty half-second jobs on ten workers take about 1 second instead of 20 × 0.5 = 10 seconds serially. This assumes the jobs mostly wait (here they sleep), so the workers do not compete for CPU; Pure-Python CPU-bound jobs in one GIL-enabled interpreter cannot run bytecode simultaneously. The later GIL unit covers native extensions and other interpreter builds. `map` returns results in input order, regardless of which finished first.

## Key takeaways
- A pool reuses a bounded number of workers rather than creating an unbounded thread per request.
- Equal-duration waiting jobs finish in whole waves; map preserves input order.
- Elapsed time depends on scheduling and overhead; the wave calculation is an ideal approximation.

## Further reading
- [pthread_create(3) — Linux manual page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/pthread_create.3.html)
- [pthread_detach(3) — Linux manual page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/pthread_detach.3.html)
- [Interlude: Thread API — OSTEP](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-api.pdf)
- [concurrent.futures — Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/library/concurrent.futures.html)
- [Python support for free threading — Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/howto/free-threading-python.html)
- [PEP 703: Making the GIL optional in CPython](https://peps.python.org/pep-0703/)

options.explanation: Only 4 jobs can run at once. The other 6 wait in the queue for a free worker.

```formula
where

N_workers: worker threads, 4 here

t_job: time for one job, 1 s here

In words: share the jobs between the workers, round up to whole waves, and each wave lasts one job.
```

5. The GIL doesn't get in the way because `time.sleep` releases it, as does real blocking I/O.

lessons.title: Size pools and avoid nested-job deadlock
lessons.summary: Start pool sizing from available compute capacity and measured waiting time.
lessons.body:
## How big should the pool be?

It depends on what the jobs spend their time doing:

- **CPU-bound** jobs (compression, image processing): start near the effective logical CPU capacity or quota, then measure. SMT, memory bandwidth, blocking, the GIL and job size can change the best size.
- **I/O-bound** jobs (waiting on network or disk): more threads than cores, so that something is computing while others wait.

Where does the I/O-bound number come from? A thread that waits 90 ms for every 10 ms it computes keeps a core busy only a tenth of the time, so you need about ten such threads per core to keep the core busy. In general, each thread keeps a core busy for its compute time divided by its total (wait plus compute) time, and the number of threads needed per core is that fraction turned upside down. A common rule of thumb follows:

```formula
N_thr = N_cpu(1 + (t_wait / t_cpu))
N_thr = 8 × (1 + 90 ms / 10 ms)
N_thr = 8 × (1 + 9) = 80
where
N_thr: the suggested number of threads in the pool
N_cpu: the number of CPU cores the pool can use, 8 here
t_wait: how long each job spends waiting (on a database, disk or network) per piece of work, in milliseconds (ms); 90 ms here
t_cpu: positive CPU-compute time per piece of work, in milliseconds (ms); 10 ms here (the estimate is undefined for zero compute time)
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
In words: the longer jobs wait compared with how long they compute, the more threads you need to keep every core busy; with no waiting at all it gives one thread per core.
```

So 8 cores and jobs that wait 90 ms on a database for every 10 ms of CPU give 80 threads. Treat it as a starting point and measure: it assumes whatever the threads wait on (the database here) can serve 80 requests at once, and it ignores memory per thread and, in Python, the GIL.

Python's own default is simpler. Since Python 3.13, `ThreadPoolExecutor` sizes itself like this when you don't pass `max_workers`:

```formula
N_max = min(32, N_cpu + 4)
N_max = min(32, 8 + 4) = 12
N_max = min(32, 64 + 4) = 32
where
N_max: the default maximum number of worker threads
min(a, b): the smaller of the two values a and b
N_cpu: the number of logical CPUs this process may use, from os.process_cpu_count() (or 1 if that is unknown); 8 and then 64 in the examples
In words: four more workers than CPUs, to cover some I/O waiting, but never more than 32.
```

In Python code that is `min(32, (os.process_cpu_count() or 1) + 4)`, which replaced the earlier formula based on `os.cpu_count()`.

> [!warning] Pool-induced deadlock
> If jobs in a pool submit child jobs to the *same* pool and wait for them, they can deadlock. With 2 workers, two parent jobs each wait for a child; both children sit in the queue with no free worker to run them. Use a separate pool for child jobs, or avoid blocking waits inside jobs.

Also watch the **queue**. An unbounded queue hides overload: under a sustained spike it grows until you run out of memory, and every queued request is already late. Bounded queues that reject or apply backpressure fail more honestly.

## Key takeaways
- Start pool sizing from available compute capacity and measured waiting time.
- The waiting-to-compute ratio is a starting estimate, subject to downstream capacity and memory limits.
- Workers waiting for queued children in the same exhausted pool can deadlock; bound queues to expose overload.

## Further reading
- [pthread_create(3) — Linux manual page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/pthread_create.3.html)
- [pthread_detach(3) — Linux manual page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/pthread_detach.3.html)
- [Interlude: Thread API — OSTEP](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-api.pdf)
- [concurrent.futures — Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/library/concurrent.futures.html)
- [Python support for free threading — Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/howto/free-threading-python.html)
- [PEP 703: Making the GIL optional in CPython](https://peps.python.org/pep-0703/)

What happens when you run this?

```python
from concurrent.futures import (
    ThreadPoolExecutor)
from threading import Barrier

    return 1

    return f.result()
```

options.text: It hangs forever
options.explanation: Correct. This is pool-induced deadlock: both workers run `parent` and wait on a `child` that is stuck in the queue because no worker is free to run it.

options.text: It raises a `RuntimeError` about deadlock
options.explanation: `ThreadPoolExecutor` doesn't detect deadlocks. The futures just never complete.

options.text: It prints `[1, 1]` but only after the 5-second switch interval
options.explanation: The switch interval (5 ms, not 5 s) governs the GIL, not the pool's queue. No worker ever becomes free.

questions.workedExample:
Trace it:

1. Both parent jobs reach the barrier, ensuring they occupy the two workers before either submits its child.
2. Each `parent` submits a `child`. Both children go into the queue.
3. Each `parent` then blocks in `f.result()` waiting for its child.
4. A child can only run on a free worker, but both workers are blocked inside `parent`.
5. Nobody can make progress: deadlock.

With 3 workers it would work, which is why this bug often hides until load increases. Fixes: a separate pool for child jobs, not blocking inside jobs (compose futures or use `asyncio`), or doing the child work inline.

lessons.title: Python’s GIL, races and parallel alternatives
lessons.summary: GIL-enabled CPython executes bytecode in one thread at a time per interpreter.
lessons.body:
## Python's GIL

A GIL-enabled CPython interpreter has a **Global Interpreter Lock**: a single lock that a thread must hold to execute Python bytecode. Python threads are real OS threads (1:1), but only one at a time runs Python code.
## Why it exists

CPython manages memory with **reference counts** on every object. Incrementing and decrementing those counts from several threads at once would need a lock or atomic operation on every object access. One big lock was simpler and made single-threaded code fast.
## What it means for CPU-bound code

```python
import threading, time

def spin(n):
    while n:
        n -= 1


# Equal work; actual durations may vary.
N = 20_000_000
t0 = time.perf_counter()
spin(N); spin(N)
dt = time.perf_counter() - t0
print(f"serial:  {dt:.2f}s")

t0 = time.perf_counter()
ts = [threading.Thread(target=spin,
                       args=(N,))
      for _ in range(2)]
for t in ts: t.start()

# Join before reading results or duration.
for t in ts: t.join()
dt = time.perf_counter() - t0
print(f"threads: {dt:.2f}s")
```

On a standard build the two lines print roughly the same time. The threads take turns holding the GIL (a waiting thread asks the holder to drop it after the **switch interval**, 5 ms by default, see `sys.getswitchinterval()`), so there is no parallel speed-up.
## What it does not hurt

The GIL is **released** during blocking I/O (`socket.recv`, file reads, `time.sleep`) and by many C extensions during long computations (NumPy array operations, `hashlib` on large inputs, `zlib`). So threads work well for I/O-bound Python, as in the pool example above, and for code that spends its time in GIL-releasing libraries.
## What it does not prevent: races

A common myth is that the GIL makes Python code thread-safe. It only guarantees that the interpreter's own internals stay consistent. Thread-switch points depend on the CPython version, and bytecodes may invoke user code or extensions. Do not assume a shared **read-modify-write** sequence is atomic:

```python
import threading

counter = 0

def bump(x):
    return x + 1

def work():
    global counter
    for _ in range(1_000_000):
        # Shared read, compute, then write.
        counter = bump(counter)

ts = [threading.Thread(target=work)
      for _ in range(4)]
for t in ts: t.start()

# Join before reading results or duration.
for t in ts: t.join()

# One observed count cannot prove safety.
print(counter)
```

This is a race demonstration, not a reproducible output guarantee. Depending on build, scheduling and implementation, it may lose updates or print the expected count; a passing run does not establish correctness. One possible interleaving is that a thread reads counter, switches before completing the call and store, and later writes back a stale value. Exact switch opportunities depend on the interpreter version; loss is possible, not guaranteed by a particular source line.

A plain `counter += 1` in the loop often *happens* to give the right answer on recent CPython versions, because of where the interpreter checks for thread switches. That is an implementation detail, not a guarantee, and it is not a safe shared-counter protocol on free-threaded builds. Protect shared state with a `threading.Lock` (the next module covers locks properly).

Some simple built-in operations have useful implementation-level locking or atomicity, but callbacks, custom key methods and free-threaded builds complicate the rules. Use documented guarantees and explicit synchronisation for shared invariants; check-then-insert is not automatically atomic.
## Getting real parallelism in Python

- **Processes**: `multiprocessing` or `ProcessPoolExecutor`. Each process has its own interpreter and GIL. The cost is pickling data between processes.
- **C extensions** that release the GIL (NumPy and friends).
- **Free-threaded CPython** ([PEP 703](https://peps.python.org/pep-0703/)): a build with no GIL, experimental in 3.13 and officially supported (but not the default) from 3.14. It's installed as a separate interpreter, e.g. `python3.14t`. Single-threaded code runs somewhat slower, and C extensions must be marked compatible or the GIL is turned back on.
- **Subinterpreters**: Python 3.14 added `concurrent.interpreters` and `InterpreterPoolExecutor`, where each interpreter has its own GIL.

> [!note] Content gap: runtime measurements
> No reproducible record supports exact thread-creation timing, a particular racy counter output, false-sharing slowdown or ideal pool speed-up. Examples show mechanisms; timing and capacity must be measured for the chosen runtime and workload.

## Key takeaways
- GIL-enabled CPython executes bytecode in one thread at a time per interpreter.
- Blocking I/O and compatible native extensions can release the GIL; multi-step shared invariants still need synchronisation.
- Processes, GIL-releasing native work, free-threaded builds and isolated interpreters offer different routes to parallel computation.

questions.prompt: Select **all** statements that are true for the standard (GIL) build of CPython.

options.text: Two threads running a pure-Python CPU-bound loop do not run in parallel
options.explanation: Correct. Only the thread holding the GIL executes bytecode, so the threads take turns.

options.text: The GIL makes `counter = bump(counter)` safe to run from several threads without a lock
options.explanation: Wrong: a thread can lose the GIL between reading `counter` and writing it back, so updates get lost. The GIL protects the interpreter, not your invariants.

options.text: The GIL is released while a thread waits in a blocking `socket.recv`
options.explanation: Correct. Blocking I/O releases the GIL, which is why threads are fine for I/O-bound Python.

options.text: A large NumPy matrix multiplication in one thread need not stop other threads running Python
options.explanation: Many numerical NumPy operations release the GIL, letting other Python threads run. This is not true for every NumPy operation; object-dtype work and callbacks need additional care.

options.text: Python threads are green threads scheduled by the interpreter, not the OS
options.explanation: Wrong: CPython threads are real OS threads (1:1). The GIL limits which one may run bytecode, but the OS schedules them.

questions.workedExample:
The GIL is one lock that must be held to **execute Python bytecode**.

1. Pure-Python CPU work: always needs the GIL, so no parallelism.
2. Blocking I/O and long C-level work that release the GIL: other threads run meanwhile.
3. Correctness: the GIL is not a portable atomicity guarantee for multi-step shared operations; switching points and extension behaviour vary.
4. Implementation: `threading.Thread` creates a real OS thread; the OS schedules it, and it then waits for the GIL.

questions.prompt: For independent pure-Python CPU-bound image jobs in one GIL-enabled CPython interpreter, which option can use multiple CPU cores, provided job sizes amortise startup and data-transfer overhead?

options.text: `ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=8)`
options.explanation: Threads share one GIL, so pure-Python CPU work runs on one core at a time. Expect roughly no speed-up.

options.text: `ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=64)`
options.explanation: More threads make it worse: still one GIL, now with more switching.

options.text: `ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=8)`
options.explanation: Correct. Each worker process has its own interpreter and its own GIL, so 8 processes can run on 8 cores. The cost is pickling the images in and the results out.

options.text: Lower `sys.setswitchinterval` so threads take turns faster
options.explanation: That changes how often the GIL changes hands, not how many threads hold it at once. It adds overhead without adding parallelism.

questions.workedExample:
1. The work is pure Python and CPU-bound, so it needs the GIL the whole time.
2. In one process, only one thread can hold the GIL at once: threads give about 1×.
3. Separate processes each have their own GIL, so 8 processes can use 8 cores.
4. Overheads: process start-up and pickling. For images, passing file paths rather than pixel data keeps that cheap.

(Alternatives: rewrite the filter with NumPy, which releases the GIL, or use a free-threaded Python build.)

lessons.title: Measure turnaround, waiting and response
lessons.summary: Response measures arrival to first service; turnaround measures arrival to completion.
lessons.body:
A machine can have more runnable threads than available logical CPUs; at other times many or all threads are asleep. The **scheduler** is the part of the kernel that decides which runnable thread gets each core next, and for how long.

Every scheduling algorithm is an answer to one question: *when the CPU becomes free, who goes next?* The answers differ because they optimise for different goals.
## What are we optimising?

| Metric | Meaning | Want |
|---|---|---|
| CPU utilisation | Fraction of time the CPU is busy | High |
| Throughput | Jobs finished per unit time | High |
| Turnaround time | Arrival to completion | Low |
| Waiting time | Time spent ready but not running | Low |
| Response time | Arrival to *first* run | Low |
| Fairness | Similar jobs get similar shares | Even |

The three times in the table are all worked out from moments on one clock that starts at 0 when we begin watching. Each is a subtraction. These identities hold for a job that never blocks, so it needs the CPU for one stretch (one CPU burst, defined in the next unit) and is either running or waiting in the queue:

```formula
T_turn = t_done − t_arrive
T_wait = T_turn − t_burst
T_resp = t_first − t_arrive
where
T_turn: the turnaround time: how long the job spent in the system, from arriving to finishing, in milliseconds (ms)
t_done: the completion time: the clock time at which the job finished, in ms
t_arrive: the arrival time: the clock time at which the job arrived and became ready to run, in ms
T_wait: the waiting time: the total time the job sat ready in the queue without running, in ms
t_burst: the burst time: how much CPU time the job needed in total, in ms
T_resp: the response time: how long the job waited before it got the CPU for the first time, in ms
t_first: the clock time at which the job first started running, in ms
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
In words: turnaround is everything from arrival to finish; take away the time the job spent actually running and what is left is time spent waiting; response time counts only the wait before the very first run.
```

For example, a job that arrives at 2 ms, first runs at 5 ms, needs 4 ms of CPU in total and finishes at 12 ms has a turnaround time of 12 − 2 = 10 ms, a waiting time of 10 − 4 = 6 ms and a response time of 5 − 2 = 3 ms. If a job also blocks for I/O, the time it spends blocked is neither running nor waiting in the ready queue, so you would subtract that too before calling the remainder "waiting".

These goals conflict. A batch system crunching overnight jobs wants **throughput** and doesn't care about response time. An interactive desktop or a web server wants **low latency**: a keypress should be handled within milliseconds even if a compile is running. Fairness can cost throughput, because switching between jobs wastes time and cache.

## Key takeaways
- Response measures arrival to first service; turnaround measures arrival to completion.
- Subtract CPU service and any blocked time to distinguish ready-queue waiting from time in the system.
- Choose metrics for the workload; fairness, overhead and throughput can conflict.

## Further reading
- [Scheduling: Introduction — OSTEP](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/cpu-sched.pdf)
- [Scheduling (computing) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scheduling_(computing))
- [Round-robin scheduling — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Round-robin_scheduling)
- [Shortest job next — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shortest_job_next)
- [Convoy effect — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convoy_effect)

questions.prompt: You are tuning the scheduler for a text editor that must react to each keypress quickly, even while a large build runs in the background. Which metric matters most?

options.text: Throughput
options.explanation: Throughput counts jobs finished per second. Maximising it favours the build, not the editor's keypress handling.

options.text: Turnaround time
options.explanation: Turnaround is arrival to completion of a whole job, which matters for batch work. A keypress handler's issue is how quickly it starts.

options.text: Response time
options.explanation: Correct. Response time is the delay from becoming ready to first getting the CPU, which is exactly what the user perceives as lag.

options.text: CPU utilisation
options.explanation: Utilisation measures how busy the CPU is. The build alone keeps it at 100%, regardless of how laggy the editor feels.

questions.workedExample:
1. The editor thread is I/O-bound: it sleeps until a key arrives, needs a fraction of a millisecond of CPU, and sleeps again.
2. What the user feels is the gap between the keypress (thread becomes ready) and the thread running: **response time**.
3. Throughput and utilisation are dominated by the build and would look fine even if the editor lagged.

That's why interactive schedulers favour threads that wake from sleep.

lessons.title: CPU bursts, blocking and preemption
lessons.summary: CPU-bound tasks compute for long bursts; I/O-bound tasks frequently block.
lessons.body:
## CPU bursts and I/O bursts

Programs alternate between using the CPU (a **CPU burst**) and waiting for something (an **I/O burst**: disk, network, keyboard, a lock).

```
CPU-bound:  [=======CPU=======]..[=====CPU
I/O-bound:  [C]......io.....[C]......io...
```

- **CPU-bound** threads (video encoding, compiling, number crunching) have long bursts and rarely block.
- **I/O-bound** threads (a shell, an editor, a web server waiting on clients) have short bursts and block often.

Burst distributions depend on workload; interactive tasks often have short bursts between waits. A good scheduler lets I/O-bound threads run promptly when they wake. They need the CPU only briefly, then go back to waiting, which keeps both the CPU and the I/O devices busy.
## Preemptive versus cooperative

The scheduler can make a decision when a thread:

1. blocks (for example on I/O) or yields;
2. finishes;
3. becomes ready (an I/O completes, a new thread is created);
4. is interrupted by the timer.

A **cooperative** (non-preemptive) scheduler only acts on 1 and 2: a thread keeps the CPU until it gives it up. Windows 3.1 and classic Mac OS worked this way, and one misbehaving program could freeze the whole machine. Today, cooperative scheduling survives *inside* programs: Python asyncio tasks yield when an await actually suspends, while event loops also move on when callbacks or coroutines return; so a coroutine stuck in a CPU loop stalls everything else in that loop.

A **preemptive** scheduler can also act on 3 and 4. A periodic **timer interrupt** returns control to the kernel, which can take the CPU away from a thread that has run long enough. Every mainstream OS (Linux, Windows, macOS) preempts user threads.

Each switch costs something: saving and restoring registers, running the scheduler, and, less visibly, cold caches and TLB for the incoming thread. There is no platform-independent switch-time constant; both direct and cache costs need measurement.

## Key takeaways
- CPU-bound tasks compute for long bursts; I/O-bound tasks frequently block.
- Cooperative execution depends on returning or suspending; a CPU loop can stall an event loop.
- Preemption lets the kernel regain control, at a workload-dependent direct and cache cost.

## Further reading
- [Scheduling: Introduction — OSTEP](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/cpu-sched.pdf)
- [Scheduling (computing) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scheduling_(computing))
- [Round-robin scheduling — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Round-robin_scheduling)
- [Shortest job next — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shortest_job_next)
- [Convoy effect — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convoy_effect)

questions.prompt: In a Python `asyncio` program, one coroutine runs a CPU-heavy loop for 2 seconds without any `await`. What happens to the other coroutines in the same event loop during those 2 seconds?

options.text: The OS preempts the coroutine every few milliseconds so the others keep running
options.explanation: The OS preempts the thread, not individual asyncio tasks. The event loop resumes other coroutines only when control returns to it; an await that completes immediately need not suspend.

options.text: asyncio automatically moves the loop to a background thread
options.explanation: asyncio does nothing of the sort. Offloading needs an explicit `run_in_executor` or `asyncio.to_thread`.

options.text: They keep running in parallel on other cores
options.explanation: An event loop runs on one thread, so its coroutines are never in parallel with each other.

options.text: They all stall until the loop finishes, because the event loop schedules cooperatively
options.explanation: Correct. This CPU loop neither returns nor suspends, so the event loop cannot resume its other tasks. An await only yields if it actually suspends; returning also gives control back.

questions.workedExample: The CPU loop does not return control to the event loop, so other coroutines in that loop stall. The OS may schedule other threads, but resuming this thread continues the same loop. Offload suitable work or yield explicitly with asyncio.sleep(0). In a GIL-enabled interpreter, to_thread can improve responsiveness but does not itself provide parallel execution of pure-Python CPU work; a process pool can.

lessons.title: Trace FCFS and the convoy effect
lessons.summary: FCFS serves arrival order without preempting a running job.
lessons.body:
## First-come, first-served (FCFS)

Run jobs in arrival order, each to completion. It's a simple FIFO queue and is non-preemptive.

Three jobs arrive at time 0 in the order P1, P2, P3, with CPU bursts of 24, 3 and 3 ms:

```
|          P1          | P2 | P3 |
0                     24   27   30
```

| Job | Burst | Waiting | Turnaround |
|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | 24 | 0 | 24 |
| P2 | 3 | 24 | 27 |
| P3 | 3 | 27 | 30 |

To compare schedules with one number, take the average waiting time: add every job's waiting time and divide by the number of jobs.

```formula
W_avg = (W_1 + W_2 + W_3) / 3
W_avg = (0 + 24 + 27) ms / 3
W_avg = 51 ms / 3 = 17 ms
where
W_avg: the average waiting time across the three jobs, in milliseconds (ms)
W_1, W_2, W_3: the waiting times of P1, P2 and P3, from the table, in ms
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
In words: add up how long each job sat in the queue and share the total equally between the jobs.
```

The average waiting time is **17 ms**. If the short jobs had arrived first (P2, P3, P1), the waits would be 0, 3 and 6 ms: an average of (0 + 3 + 6) / 3 = **3 ms**. Same work, nearly six times better.

This is the **convoy effect**: short jobs stuck behind a long one, like cars behind a lorry on a single-lane road. With a mix of one CPU-bound and several I/O-bound threads, the I/O-bound ones queue behind the hog while the disks sit idle, then all finish their I/O together while the CPU sits idle.

## Key takeaways
- FCFS serves arrival order without preempting a running job.
- Short jobs behind a long CPU burst suffer the convoy effect.
- Compute waiting times from the stated arrivals and schedule before averaging them.

## Further reading
- [Scheduling: Introduction — OSTEP](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/cpu-sched.pdf)
- [Scheduling (computing) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scheduling_(computing))
- [Round-robin scheduling — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Round-robin_scheduling)
- [Shortest job next — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shortest_job_next)
- [Convoy effect — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convoy_effect)

questions.prompt: Jobs A (5 ms), B (2 ms) and C (3 ms) all arrive at time 0 and are scheduled **FCFS** in the order A, B, C. What is the average waiting time?

options.text: 4 ms
options.explanation: Correct. A waits 0, B waits 5 (behind A), C waits 7 (behind A and B): (0 + 5 + 7) / 3 = 4 ms.
That is the burst average, (5 + 2 + 3) / 3. Waiting time is time spent queued, not running.
That's the average **turnaround** time: (5 + 7 + 10) / 3. Waiting time excludes each job's own burst.
That's what SJF would give (B, C, A: waits 0, 2, 5 → 7/3). The question says FCFS in the order A, B, C.

questions.workedExample:
Draw the Gantt chart:

```
|   A   | B |  C  |
0       5   7    10
```

Each job runs in one piece, so its waiting time is its start time minus its arrival time:

| Job | Start | Wait |
|---|---|---|
| A | 0 | 0 |
| B | 5 | 5 |
| C | 7 | 7 |

```formula
W = t_start − t_arrive
W_avg = (W_A + W_B + W_C) / 3
W_avg = (0 + 5 + 7) ms / 3
W_avg = 12 ms / 3 = 4 ms
where
W: a job's waiting time, in milliseconds (ms)
t_start: the clock time at which the job starts running, from the chart, in ms
t_arrive: the clock time at which the job arrives; 0 ms for all three here
W_A, W_B, W_C: the waiting times of A, B and C, in ms
W_avg: the average waiting time over the three jobs, in ms
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
In words: each job waits from its arrival until it starts; add the waits and divide by the number of jobs.
```

The average waiting time is **4 ms**. Running the shortest first (B, C, A) would give waits of 0, 2 and 5 ms, an average of 7 / 3 ≈ 2.33 ms.

questions.prompt: Under **FCFS**, one CPU-bound job (100 ms bursts) shares a machine with five I/O-bound jobs (1 ms of CPU, then a disk read). What happens, and what helps most?

options.text: Nothing bad: FCFS is fair because everyone eventually runs
options.explanation: Everyone runs eventually, but in convoys: the disk idles while I/O jobs queue behind the 100 ms burst, then the CPU idles while they all do I/O.

options.text: Short I/O-bound jobs can wait behind the long CPU burst while the disk is idle; preemptive time slicing can reduce that convoy delay
options.explanation: The convoy effect delays short bursts. Preemption gives them earlier opportunities to issue I/O; actual CPU/disk utilisation depends on all burst and I/O timings.

options.text: The CPU-bound job starves, because the five I/O-bound jobs outnumber it
options.explanation: FCFS runs whoever is first in the queue; numbers don't matter. The CPU-bound job, if anything, does too well.

options.text: Increase the quantum so that each job runs longer
options.explanation: FCFS has no quantum. And under RR, a bigger quantum moves it back towards FCFS, worsening the convoy.

questions.workedExample: A short I/O-bound burst that becomes ready during the long FCFS burst waits until that burst finishes. Until it runs and issues its next read, the disk may be idle. Several waiting jobs can then issue reads in a cluster. Exact CPU and disk utilisation needs the omitted disk-service times. Under an ideal round-robin model with a 10 ms quantum, short bursts can run after the current quantum and other queued bursts, rather than after a whole 100 ms CPU burst. This can reduce the convoy delay; no fixed throughput gain or disk-idle fraction follows from the supplied numbers alone.

lessons.title: Trace SJF and shortest remaining time
lessons.summary: Non-preemptive SJF selects the shortest available burst and then lets it finish.
lessons.body:
## Shortest job first (SJF)

Always run the job with the **shortest next CPU burst**. When all jobs are available at once, SJF is provably optimal for average waiting time: moving a short job ahead of a long one reduces the short job's wait by more than it increases the long one's.

Now use staggered arrivals:

| Job | Arrival | Burst |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | 0 | 8 |
| P2 | 1 | 4 |
| P3 | 2 | 9 |
| P4 | 3 | 5 |

**Non-preemptive SJF.** At time 0 only P1 is there, so it runs to completion. At 8, P2 (4), P3 (9) and P4 (5) are waiting; the shortest is P2, then P4, then P3.

```
|   P1   |  P2  |  P4  |    P3    |
0        8     12     17         26
```

Each job runs in one piece, so its waiting time is simply its start time minus its arrival time:

```formula
W = t_start − t_arrive
W_P1 = (0 − 0) ms = 0 ms
W_P2 = (8 − 1) ms = 7 ms
W_P4 = (12 − 3) ms = 9 ms
W_P3 = (17 − 2) ms = 15 ms
W_avg = (0 + 7 + 9 + 15) ms / 4
W_avg = 31 ms / 4 = 7.75 ms
where
W: a job's waiting time, in milliseconds (ms)
t_start: the clock time at which the job starts running, read off the chart, in ms
t_arrive: the clock time at which the job arrives, from the table, in ms
W_P1, W_P2, W_P3, W_P4: the waiting times of P1, P2, P3 and P4, in ms
W_avg: the average waiting time over the four jobs, in ms
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
In words: a job that is never interrupted waits only once, from its arrival until it starts, so subtract one from the other and average over the jobs.
```

The average waiting time is **7.75 ms**.
## Shortest remaining time first (SRTF)

The preemptive version: whenever a job arrives, compare its burst with the *remaining* time of the running job, and switch if it's shorter.

1. At 0 ms: P1 starts (remaining 8).
2. At 1 ms: P2 arrives needing 4, less than P1's remaining 7. Preempt; P2 runs.
3. At 2 ms and 3 ms: P3 (9) and P4 (5) arrive; neither beats P2's remaining 3 or 2.
4. At 5 ms: P2 done. Remaining: P1 7, P3 9, P4 5. P4 runs.
5. At 10 ms: P4 done. P1 (7) runs, then P3.

```
|P1| P2 |  P4  |   P1   |   P3    |
0  1    5     10       17        26
```

A preempted job can wait in several pieces (P1 waits from 1 to 10 ms), so "start minus arrival" no longer works. Instead take the job's whole time in the system and subtract the time it actually ran:

```formula
W = T_turn − t_burst
T_turn = t_done − t_arrive
W_P1 = ((17 − 0) − 8) ms = 9 ms
W_P2 = ((5 − 1) − 4) ms = 0 ms
W_P3 = ((26 − 2) − 9) ms = 15 ms
W_P4 = ((10 − 3) − 5) ms = 2 ms
W_avg = (9 + 0 + 15 + 2) ms / 4
W_avg = 26 ms / 4 = 6.5 ms
where
W: a job's total waiting time, in milliseconds (ms)
T_turn: the job's turnaround time, from arrival to completion, in ms
t_burst: the CPU time the job needs in total, from the table, in ms
t_done: the clock time at which the job finishes, read off the chart, in ms
t_arrive: the clock time at which the job arrives, from the table, in ms
W_P1, W_P2, W_P3, W_P4: the waiting times of P1, P2, P3 and P4, in ms
W_avg: the average waiting time over the four jobs, in ms
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
In words: everything a job spends in the system that is not running is waiting, however many pieces it comes in.
```

The average is **6.5 ms**, better than non-preemptive SJF.

## Key takeaways
- Non-preemptive SJF selects the shortest available burst and then lets it finish.
- SRTF can preempt when a newly arrived burst is shorter than the running job’s remaining work.
- For a job that never blocks, waiting is turnaround minus total CPU service, even after preemptions.

## Further reading
- [Scheduling: Introduction — OSTEP](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/cpu-sched.pdf)
- [Scheduling (computing) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scheduling_(computing))
- [Round-robin scheduling — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Round-robin_scheduling)
- [Shortest job next — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shortest_job_next)
- [Convoy effect — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convoy_effect)
