```formula
t_burst: the CPU time the job needs in total
W_A, W_B, W_C, W_D: the waiting times of A, B, C and D
W_avg: the average waiting time over the four jobs
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
In words: time in the system minus time spent running is time spent waiting, however many pieces it comes in.
```

The average waiting time is **3.5**.

lessons.title: Predict bursts and understand SJF’s limits
lessons.summary: Exponential averaging blends the measured burst with the previous prediction.
lessons.body:
## The catch: you don't know the future

The OS can't know how long a burst will be. It can **predict** from history. Threads tend to behave like they did recently, so a common textbook method is an **exponential average**: after each burst, blend the burst that just happened with the previous prediction.

```formula
τ_{n+1} = αt_n + (1 − α)τ_n
τ_1 = 10 ms
τ_2 = 0.5 × 6 ms + 0.5 × 10 ms = 8 ms
τ_3 = 0.5 × 4 ms + 0.5 × 8 ms = 6 ms
where
τ_{n+1}: tau, the predicted length of the next CPU burst, in milliseconds (ms)
t_n: the measured length of the burst that just finished, in ms; here t_1 = 6 ms and then t_2 = 4 ms
τ_n: the previous prediction, the one made for the burst that just finished, in ms
α: alpha, the weight given to the latest burst, between 0 and 1; 0.5 here. Near 1, the prediction follows the last burst closely; near 0, it barely changes
τ_1: the initial guess before any burst has been measured, 10 ms here
τ_2, τ_3: the second and third predictions, in ms
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
In words: the next prediction is part the latest real burst and part the old prediction; with α = 0.5 it is exactly halfway between the two.
```

It is called exponential because each update multiplies older contributions by the complement of the latest-burst weight. With the weight set to one half, the burst before last counts a quarter, the one before that an eighth, and so on. For a fixed weight strictly between zero and one, old contributions approach zero without reaching it in exact arithmetic. At a weight of one, only the latest burst counts; at zero, the prediction never updates. The method works only as well as the past predicts the future; a thread that suddenly changes behaviour is mispredicted for a few bursts.

SJF also risks **starvation**: if short jobs keep arriving, a long job may never run. The next lesson covers how real schedulers avoid that.

## Key takeaways
- Exponential averaging blends the measured burst with the previous prediction.
- The newest burst’s weight controls how quickly the estimate adapts.
- Known-burst SJF results depend on the arrival and cost model; repeated short arrivals can starve a long job.

## Further reading
- [Scheduling: Introduction — OSTEP](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/cpu-sched.pdf)
- [Scheduling (computing) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scheduling_(computing))
- [Round-robin scheduling — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Round-robin_scheduling)
- [Shortest job next — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shortest_job_next)
- [Convoy effect — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convoy_effect)

options.explanation: Correct. Any schedule that runs a longer job before a shorter one can be improved by exchanging them.

options.text: A real OS must estimate burst lengths, for example from past bursts
options.explanation: Correct. The scheduler can't see the future; it predicts, typically with an exponential average of previous bursts.

options.text: Long jobs can starve if short jobs keep arriving
options.explanation: Correct. A steady stream of short jobs always beats the long one, which may wait indefinitely.

options.text: It gives long jobs good response time

```formula
τ_2 = 0.5 × 4 ms + 0.5 × 12 ms = 8 ms
τ_3 = 0.5 × 8 ms + 0.5 × 8 ms = 8 ms
τ_4 = 0.5 × 2 ms + 0.5 × 8 ms = 5 ms

where
```

lessons.title: Round robin: response versus switching cost
lessons.summary: Round robin rotates runnable jobs after a quantum and lets short bursts finish early.
lessons.body:
## Round robin (RR)

Give each job a fixed **time quantum** (time slice), then preempt it and put it at the back of the ready queue. RR is FCFS plus a timer, and it is the basis of most interactive scheduling.

Back to P1 = 24, P2 = 3 and P3 = 3, all at time 0, with a quantum of 4 ms:

```
| P1 | P2 | P3 |          P1          |
0    4    7   10                     30
```

P2 and P3 finish within their first quantum and leave early. P1 then runs alone, quantum after quantum.

| Job | Waiting | Turnaround | Response |
|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | 6 | 30 | 0 |
| P2 | 4 | 7 | 4 |
| P3 | 7 | 10 | 7 |

Averaging the columns:

```formula
W_avg = (6 + 4 + 7) ms / 3 = 17 ms / 3
W_avg ≈ 5.67 ms
R_avg = (0 + 4 + 7) ms / 3 = 11 ms / 3
R_avg ≈ 3.67 ms
where
W_avg: the average waiting time of the three jobs, in milliseconds (ms)
R_avg: the average response time: for each job, the clock time of its first run minus its arrival time (0 ms for all three), averaged, in ms
≈: approximately equal to (rounded to two decimal places)
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
In words: round robin gets every job started quickly, which is what the low average response time measures.
```

Average waiting is about **5.67 ms** and average response time about **3.67 ms**, against 17 ms and 17 ms for FCFS in the original order (under FCFS a job's first run is also its only run, so its response time equals its waiting time).

> [!note] A tie-breaking convention
> When a job's quantum expires at the same moment a new job arrives, most textbooks put the new arrival in the queue first, then the preempted job. State your convention when you work these by hand; it can change the answer.
## Choosing the quantum

- **Too large**, and RR degenerates into FCFS: interactive jobs wait behind CPU hogs.
- **Too small**, and the CPU spends its time switching.

To see how much is wasted, assume every job uses its full quantum, so each quantum of useful work is followed by one context switch. The wasted fraction is the switch time divided by the whole cycle:

```formula
f = s / (q + s)
f = 0.1 ms / (10 ms + 0.1 ms) ≈ 0.0099
f = 0.1 ms / (1 ms + 0.1 ms) ≈ 0.091
where
f: the fraction of CPU time spent switching rather than running jobs (multiply by 100 for a percentage)
s: the time one context switch takes, in milliseconds (ms); 0.1 ms is an assumed illustrative figure, not a measurement
q: the time quantum, in ms
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
In words: the shorter the quantum, the bigger the share of each cycle that goes on switching.
```

With a 0.1 ms switch cost, a 10 ms quantum wastes about 1% and a 1 ms quantum about 9%, before counting cache effects.

Choose the quantum from measured burst lengths, latency goals and overhead. No workload trace or platform-specific measurement is supplied to justify a universal percentile target or slice range here.

RR has good response time and is fair, but its **average turnaround** can be poor when jobs are of similar length: with three 10 ms jobs and a 1 ms quantum, all three finish near 30 ms, whereas FCFS finishes them at 10, 20 and 30.
## Comparison

| Algorithm | Preemptive | Strength | Weakness |
|---|---|---|---|
| FCFS | No | Simple, no starvation | Convoy effect |
| SJF | No | Optimal avg wait | Needs burst length; starvation |
| SRTF | Yes | Even better avg wait | Same, plus more switches |
| RR | Yes | Response time, fairness | Turnaround; quantum tuning |

No real general-purpose OS uses any of these alone. Linux, Windows and macOS combine their ideas: priorities, time slices, and rewarding threads that block a lot. The following lessons build up to what Linux actually does.

## Key takeaways
- Round robin rotates runnable jobs after a quantum and lets short bursts finish early.
- State how arrivals and expired quanta are ordered when their timestamps tie.
- Small quanta improve first response but increase switching overhead; similar jobs can finish later overall.

## Further reading
- [Scheduling: Introduction — OSTEP](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/cpu-sched.pdf)
- [Scheduling (computing) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scheduling_(computing))
- [Round-robin scheduling — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Round-robin_scheduling)
- [Shortest job next — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shortest_job_next)
- [Convoy effect — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convoy_effect)

That's when A, the longest job, finishes.

```formula

where

q: the round-robin quantum, 4.5 ms here
```

questions.prompt: Three jobs, each needing 10 ms of CPU, arrive at time 0. Compare FCFS with round robin using a 1 ms quantum, ignoring switch costs. Select **all** true statements.

options.text: RR's average turnaround time is higher than FCFS's
options.explanation: Correct. FCFS finishes them at 10, 20 and 30 (average 20). RR finishes them at 28, 29 and 30 (average 29).

options.text: RR's average response time is lower than FCFS's
options.explanation: Correct. RR starts them at 0, 1 and 2 (average 1); FCFS at 0, 10 and 20 (average 10).

options.text: Both finish all the work at time 30
options.explanation: Correct. With no switch costs, the CPU is busy for 30 ms either way; only the order changes.

options.text: RR has higher throughput

questions.workedExample:
**FCFS**:

```
|   A    |   B    |   C    |
0       10       20       30
```

Turnarounds 10, 20, 30 → average 20. Responses 0, 10, 20 → average 10.

**RR with a 1 ms quantum**: A, B, C, A, B, C, ... Each job's 10th slice comes in the last round:

- A's last slice: 27–28
- B's: 28–29
- C's: 29–30

Turnarounds 28, 29, 30 → average 29. Responses 0, 1, 2 → average 1.

So RR trades turnaround for response time. When jobs are equal in length, slicing them finely makes *everyone* finish late.

lessons.title: Strict priorities and aging
lessons.summary: Strict priority can starve lower-priority work; Linux nice values instead express fair weights.
lessons.body:
FCFS, SJF and round robin treat all jobs as equals. Real systems don't: an audio thread that misses a 5 ms deadline produces a click, while a backup job can wait. **Priority scheduling** lets the system express that. It also introduces two classic failure modes, **starvation** and **priority inversion**, and the multilevel feedback queue adapts scheduling to observed behaviour. Priority inheritance addresses lock-related priority inversion separately.
## Priority scheduling

In a strict-priority model, the scheduler chooses the highest-priority ready thread. Linux nice values instead set relative fair-scheduling weights; they are not strict priorities. Threads of equal priority usually share the CPU round robin. With preemption, a higher-priority thread that becomes ready takes the CPU immediately.

Conventions vary, so always check which way the numbers run:

| System | Range | Higher priority is |
|---|---|---|
| Linux nice | −20 to 19 | Lower number |
| Linux real-time | 1 to 99 | Higher number |
| Windows | 0 to 31 | Higher number |

There are **static priorities** (set once by the user or administrator) and **dynamic priorities** (adjusted by the OS based on behaviour). SJF is in fact a priority scheduler whose priority is the predicted burst length.
## Starvation and aging

Strict priority has an obvious hole: if high-priority work keeps arriving, low-priority work **never runs**. That is **starvation**.

> [!note] Content gap: unverified historical anecdote
> A commonly repeated story about a job waiting for years on an early time-sharing system has been omitted because this audit could not establish a reliable primary record. The starvation mechanism does not depend on that story.

The standard cure is **aging**: increase a thread's priority the longer it waits, so that eventually it beats the steady stream of newcomers.
## How long does aging take?

Suppose priority numbers run from 0 (highest) to 127 (lowest), and a waiting thread improves by one level every second. A thread at 127 competes with a constant load at priority 20. The wait is the number of levels it must climb times the time each level takes:

```formula
t_age = (p_start − p_load)t_step
t_age = (127 − 20) × 1 s = 107 s
where
t_age: how long the thread waits before it reaches the same priority as the competing work, in seconds (s)
p_start: the waiting thread's starting priority number, 127 here (the lowest priority)
p_load: the priority number of the steady competing load, 20 here
t_step: how long the thread must wait to improve by one level, 1 s here
s: seconds
In words: count the levels the thread has to climb, then multiply by how long each level takes.
```

So it reaches equal priority after 107 seconds. Actual first service also depends on tie-breaking and queue length, and a chosen policy may reset the priority after the thread has run.

## Key takeaways
- Strict priority can starve lower-priority work; Linux nice values instead express fair weights.
- Check whether a larger numeric priority means more or less importance.
- Aging can raise waiting work to a competing priority; first service still depends on ties and queued work.

## Further reading
- [Scheduling: The Multi-Level Feedback Queue — OSTEP](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/cpu-sched-mlfq.pdf)
- [Glenn Reeves: what happened on Pathfinder — firsthand correction in RISKS](https://catless.ncl.ac.uk/Risks/19.54.html)
- [Priority inversion — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Priority_inversion)
- [Priority inheritance — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Priority_inheritance)
- [RT-mutex subsystem with PI support — Linux kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/locking/rt-mutex.html)
- [Multilevel feedback queue — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multilevel_feedback_queue)

options.explanation: That's the convention for Linux real-time priorities (1–99) and Windows, not for nice values. Nice runs the other way: a 'nicer' process is more generous to others.

options.explanation: I/O priority is a separate setting (ionice). Nice directly changes the CPU share a thread gets.

options.text: Neither; nice values only matter for real-time threads
options.explanation: It's the reverse: nice applies to normal (non-real-time) threads. Real-time threads use a separate 1–99 priority.

Lower nice means greater fair-scheduling weight, so the nice −5 task receives more long-run CPU service than the nice 10 task under the specified same-group contention. questions.prompt: A strict, preemptive priority scheduler runs a steady stream of high-priority web requests. A low-priority log-cleanup job has been ready for an hour and has never run. What is this called, and what is the classic fix?

options.text: Priority inversion; fix it with priority inheritance
options.explanation: Inversion is when a high-priority thread is stuck behind lower-priority ones because of a lock. Here no lock is involved: the low-priority job is simply always outranked.

options.text: Deadlock; fix it by ordering lock acquisition
options.explanation: Deadlock needs a cycle of threads waiting on each other. The web requests are making progress; only the low-priority job is stuck.

options.text: Starvation; fix it with aging
options.explanation: Correct. The job is perpetually outranked, which is starvation. Aging raises its priority the longer it waits until it eventually wins.

options.text: Convoy effect; fix it with a shorter quantum
options.explanation: The convoy effect is short jobs stuck behind a long one under FCFS. Changing the quantum doesn't help a job that is never selected at all.

questions.workedExample:
1. No circular blocking dependency is described: high-priority requests keep running while cleanup remains ready. Deadlock can involve resources other than locks, but that is not the mechanism here.
2. Is the job ready but never chosen because higher-priority work keeps arriving? Yes. That is **starvation**.
3. The fix must eventually let the job win. **Aging** does this: each second it waits, its priority improves, until it outranks the newcomers, runs, and drops back.

MLFQ's periodic priority boost is another cure for the same problem.

questions.prompt: Priorities run from 0 (highest) to 127. A waiting thread improves by one level every 2 seconds, starting at 100. How long until it reaches the same priority as work arriving at priority 40?

options.text: About 60 seconds
options.explanation: That's the number of levels to climb (100 − 40 = 60), but it forgets that each level takes 2 seconds.

options.text: About 120 seconds
options.explanation: Correct. It must climb 60 levels at 2 seconds each: 60 × 2 = 120 seconds.

options.text: About 200 seconds
options.explanation: Aging lowers the numeric priority under this model. The question asks when it reaches 40; actual service also depends on the runnable queue and tie-breaking.

options.text: Never, because the stream never stops
options.explanation: That would be true without aging. Aging is exactly what guarantees it eventually runs.

questions.workedExample:
Count the levels to climb, then multiply by the time per level:

```formula
Δp = p_start − p_load = 100 − 40 = 60
t_age = Δp t_step
t_age = 60 × 2 s = 120 s
where
Δp: delta p, the number of priority levels the thread must climb
p_start: the thread's starting priority number, 100
p_load: the priority number of the arriving work, 40
t_age: the time until the thread reaches priority 40, in seconds (s)
t_step: the time to improve by one level, 2 s
s: seconds
In words: 60 levels at 2 seconds each takes 120 seconds.
```

That establishes equal priority, not an exact first-run time. Tie-breaking, queue length and scheduling overhead determine when it actually runs.

lessons.title: Learn job behaviour with feedback queues
lessons.summary: New jobs start at the top so genuinely short jobs can finish promptly.
lessons.body:
## The multilevel feedback queue (MLFQ)

The deeper problem is that the OS doesn't know which jobs are short or interactive. SJF needs that knowledge; round robin ignores it. The **multilevel feedback queue**, first described by Corbató's CTSS in 1962 (part of the work that earned him the Turing Award), *learns* it by watching how jobs behave.

MLFQ keeps several ready queues, one per priority level. The textbook rules (as in OSTEP) are:

1. If job A has a higher priority than job B, A runs.
2. If A and B have the same priority, they share the CPU round robin.
3. A new job enters at the **highest** priority.
4. Once a job uses up its **time allotment** at a level, however many times it gave up the CPU along the way, it moves down one level.
5. After a fixed period (the boost period), move **every** job back to the top queue (the **priority boost**).

Lower queues usually get **longer quanta**: short slices at the top for responsiveness, long slices at the bottom where CPU-bound jobs live and switching overhead matters more.

```
Q2 (high)  10 ms slice  [new, interactive]
Q1         20 ms slice  [demoted once]
Q0 (low)   40 ms slice  [CPU-bound, RR]
```
## Why it approximates SJF

Rule 3 assumes every new job might be short. If it is, it finishes (or blocks) while still at the top, getting SJF-like treatment. If it isn't, Rule 4 pushes it down level by level until it sits with the other long jobs. The scheduler has learned the job is CPU-bound without being told.
## A worked trace

Three levels as above, with an allotment of one quantum per level. A CPU-bound job A arrives at 0. An interactive job B arrives at 50 and repeatedly runs for 2 ms, then waits 8 ms for I/O.

```
ms      0   10        30   50 52   60 62
Q2      [A ]               [B]     [B]
Q1          [A     ]
Q0                  [A   ]    [A  ]   [A
```

1. 0–10: A uses its full 10 ms at Q2 and is demoted.
2. 10–30: A uses 20 ms at Q1 and is demoted to Q0.
3. 30–50: A runs at Q0.
4. 50: B arrives at Q2 and preempts A immediately (Rule 1).
5. B runs 2 ms and blocks; A carries on until B's I/O completes at 60, when B preempts it again.

In the idealised zero-overhead trace, B runs immediately when ready; no measured wake-up latency is implied. A uses all the leftover time. That's the behaviour we want from a desktop.

## Key takeaways
- New jobs start at the top so genuinely short jobs can finish promptly.
- CPU-heavy jobs sink through queues with longer slices.
- Higher-priority arrivals preempt lower queues in the stated idealised policy.

## Further reading
- [Scheduling: The Multi-Level Feedback Queue — OSTEP](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/cpu-sched-mlfq.pdf)
- [Glenn Reeves: what happened on Pathfinder — firsthand correction in RISKS](https://catless.ncl.ac.uk/Risks/19.54.html)

- [Priority inheritance — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Priority_inheritance)

options.text: In the middle queue, as a neutral guess
options.explanation: MLFQ deliberately makes an optimistic guess, not a neutral one. A middle start would delay short interactive jobs.

options.explanation: MLFQ exists precisely because the OS doesn't know run times. Jobs don't declare them.

2. A short or interactive job finishes or blocks while still at the top, so it gets fast service.
3. A long CPU-bound job uses up its allotment and sinks level by level (Rule 4) until it sits with the other long jobs.

The scheduler learns each job's character from its behaviour.

options.explanation: That's when B becomes ready for its second burst. It has used only 2 ms of its 10 ms allotment so far.

options.text: At 52 ms
options.explanation: That's the end of B's first burst. Blocking doesn't demote a job under Rule 4; only using the full allotment does.

options.text: At 100 ms
options.explanation: The fifth burst ends at 92; 100 is eight milliseconds later, when the next burst becomes ready after its I/O wait.

options.text: At 92 ms
options.explanation: Correct. Bursts run 50–52, 60–62, 70–72, 80–82, 90–92. After the fifth, B has used 10 ms at the top level and is demoted at 92 ms.

questions.workedExample:
B preempts A each time it becomes ready, so its bursts run immediately:

| Burst | Runs | Total used |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 50–52 | 2 ms |
| 2 | 60–62 | 4 ms |
| 3 | 70–72 | 6 ms |
| 4 | 80–82 | 8 ms |
| 5 | 90–92 | 10 ms |

Each cycle is 2 ms of CPU plus 8 ms of I/O. Burst number n starts n − 1 cycles after B arrives, so the fifth burst ends at:

```formula
T_cyc = t_b + t_io
T_cyc = 2 ms + 8 ms = 10 ms
t_end = t_arr + (n − 1)T_cyc + t_b
t_end = 50 ms + 4 × 10 ms + 2 ms
t_end = 92 ms
where
T_cyc: the length of one run-then-wait cycle, in milliseconds (ms)
t_b: the CPU time B uses per burst, 2 ms
t_io: B's I/O wait after each burst, 8 ms
t_end: the time at which burst n ends, in ms
t_arr: when B arrives, 50 ms
n: the burst number, 5 here (5 × 2 ms uses the whole 10 ms allotment)
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
In words: four full cycles after arriving, B starts its fifth burst at 90 ms, and 2 ms later its allotment is spent.
```

So at **92 ms** it moves to the 20 ms queue. A has long since sunk to the bottom (demoted at 10 and 30), so B still beats it.

lessons.title: Prevent gaming and starvation in MLFQ
lessons.summary: Count cumulative CPU consumption at a level, not just the latest uninterrupted burst.
lessons.body:
## Rule 4 and gaming the scheduler

Early MLFQ designs had a gentler rule: *a job that gives up the CPU before its quantum expires keeps its priority*. That rewards interactive jobs, but it can be **gamed**. A job that runs for 9.9 ms of a 10 ms quantum, then issues a trivial I/O, stays at the top forever and gets nearly all the CPU.

Rule 4 closes the hole with better **accounting**: the scheduler tracks *total* CPU used at a level, not per burst. In the preceding feedback-trace unit, B uses 2 ms per burst. Dividing its allotment by the CPU it uses per burst gives the number of bursts before it is demoted:

```formula
n_bursts = A_level / t_burst
n_bursts = 10 ms / 2 ms = 5
where
n_bursts: how many bursts B can run at the top level before it is demoted
A_level: the time allotment at the top level, 10 ms here
t_burst: the CPU time B uses in each burst, 2 ms here
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
In words: B's short bursts add up, and after five of them it has spent its whole allotment.
```

So after five bursts B drops to Q1. That is the cost of being game-proof: even a genuinely interactive job slowly sinks. Rule 5 lifts it back.
## Rule 5: the priority boost

Without boosts, two things go wrong:

- **Starvation**: many interactive jobs at the top can use all the CPU, and jobs in Q0 never run.
- **Changing behaviour**: a job that was CPU-bound (say, a program loading data) and then becomes interactive is stuck at the bottom.

Boosting everything to the top once every boost period fixes both. The length of that period is one of Ousterhout's "voodoo constants": too long and long jobs starve; too short and interactive jobs lose their advantage. Real systems tune it, or replace the boost with aging or decay of usage history.
## MLFQ in real systems

The cited historical Solaris documentation describes 60 time-sharing priorities and default quanta from 40 ms at priority 59 to 200 ms at priority 0; these are version/configuration-specific values. Windows uses 32 priority levels with dynamic boosts for threads that finish waiting on I/O or own the foreground window. FreeBSD's ULE scheduler computes an "interactivity score" from sleep and run times. Linux took a different route: since 2.6.23 (2007) its normal scheduler has been built on fairness rather than feedback queues, as the next lesson explains.

## Key takeaways
- Count cumulative CPU consumption at a level, not just the latest uninterrupted burst.
- Periodic boosts let long-waiting jobs run and let changed workloads regain priority.
- Queue counts, quanta and boost intervals are policy choices; historical system examples have version-specific values.

## Further reading
- [Scheduling: The Multi-Level Feedback Queue — OSTEP](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/cpu-sched-mlfq.pdf)
- [Glenn Reeves: what happened on Pathfinder — firsthand correction in RISKS](https://catless.ncl.ac.uk/Risks/19.54.html)
- [Priority inversion — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Priority_inversion)
- [Priority inheritance — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Priority_inheritance)
- [RT-mutex subsystem with PI support — Linux kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/locking/rt-mutex.html)
- [Multilevel feedback queue — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multilevel_feedback_queue)

questions.prompt: An MLFQ uses the **old** rule: a job that gives up the CPU before its 10 ms quantum expires keeps its priority. A malicious job runs for 9.9 ms, then does a trivial 0.1 ms I/O, and repeats. Two honest CPU-bound jobs are in the bottom queue. Roughly what share of the CPU does the malicious job get?

options.text: About one third, like the others
options.explanation: That would be fair sharing, but the attacker never leaves the top queue, so it always outranks the honest jobs.

options.text: About half
options.explanation: There's no mechanism here that splits the CPU evenly between the top queue and the rest.

options.text: Almost all of it (around 99%)
options.explanation: Correct. It stays at the top forever and preempts the bottom queue whenever it's ready. The honest jobs only run during its 0.1 ms I/O gaps.

options.text: None, because I/O demotes it
options.explanation: Under the old rule, giving up the CPU early is rewarded, not punished. That's the hole.

questions.workedExample:
1. Under the old rule the attacker never uses a full quantum, so it never moves down.
2. Top-queue jobs always beat bottom-queue jobs (Rule 1).
3. The attacker is runnable 9.9 ms of every 10 ms:

```formula
f = t_run / (t_run + t_io)
f = 9.9 ms / (9.9 ms + 0.1 ms)
f = 9.9 ms / 10 ms = 0.99 = 99 %
where
f: the attacker's share of the CPU
t_run: how long it runs in each cycle, 9.9 ms
t_io: its trivial I/O pause in each cycle, 0.1 ms
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
%: per cent, hundredths: 0.99 = 99 %
In words: the attacker is ready to run for 99 of every 100 milliseconds, and whenever it is ready it wins.
```

So it gets about **99%**.
4. The honest jobs share the remaining ~1%.

The new Rule 4 fixes this by counting *total* CPU used at a level: after about one allotment's worth of CPU (10 ms), the attacker is demoted however many times it yielded.

That would require 1 ms bursts. With 2 ms bursts, 10 ms is reached after 5.

```formula
where
```

questions.prompt: Which problems does MLFQ's periodic **priority boost** (Rule 5) solve? Select all that apply.

options.text: Jobs in the bottom queue starving when many interactive jobs fill the top
options.explanation: Boosting gives low-queue jobs access to the top queue again. With fair queue ordering it combats starvation, but service within every boost period is not guaranteed when the runnable queue is large.

options.text: A job that was CPU-bound becoming interactive but staying stuck at the bottom
options.explanation: Correct. The boost gives it another chance to show its new behaviour from the top queue.

options.text: Unbounded priority inversion on a mutex
options.explanation: Inversion is a lock problem, fixed by priority inheritance or ceilings. A boost every so many milliseconds doesn't bound how long a high-priority thread waits on a lock.

lessons.title: Priority inversion and inherited lock priority
lessons.summary: A medium-priority task can delay a high-priority waiter by preempting its low-priority lock holder.
lessons.body:
## Priority inversion

Priorities interact badly with locks. Take three threads on one CPU, sharing a mutex `m`:

- **H**: high priority, needs `m` briefly;
- **M**: medium priority, CPU-heavy, never touches `m`;
- **L**: low priority, takes `m` now and then.

```
L: lock(m) ...........   ...unlock
H:      wakes, lock(m) -> BLOCKED
M:           wakes, runs, runs, runs
           <---- H waits for M ---->
```

1. L takes `m`.
2. H wakes, preempts L and tries to lock `m`. It blocks.
3. M wakes. It outranks L, so it preempts L.
4. L can't run, so it can't release `m`, so H can't run.

H is now waiting for M, a lower-priority thread that has nothing to do with `m`. The priorities have been **inverted**. Worse, the delay isn't bounded by L's short critical section; it lasts as long as M (and any other medium-priority work) keeps running. This is **unbounded priority inversion**.
## Mars Pathfinder, 1997

Glenn Reeves, who led Pathfinder's software team, describes a priority inversion involving a semaphore inside VxWorks `select`/pipe handling. The low-priority ASI/MET task held the resource; intermediate work delayed it while the higher-priority `bc_dist` task waited. A deadline check by `bc_sched` triggered a reset.

Engineers reproduced the failure with tracing, enabled priority inheritance through a configuration change, tested the wider effects and deployed it using their validated spacecraft patch mechanism. Reeves explicitly says they **did not use the VxWorks shell** for the update. He also says the pre-landing occurrence was investigated and remained unresolved, rather than being dismissed as a hardware glitch.

This firsthand correction matters: retain the inversion lesson without repeating the inaccurate interpreter-fix and ignored-warning story.
## Priority inheritance

The fix is **priority inheritance**: while a thread holds a lock that a higher-priority thread is waiting for, it temporarily runs at the waiter's priority.

1. H blocks on `m`, held by L. L is boosted to H's priority.
2. M wakes but can't preempt L, which now outranks it.
3. L finishes its critical section and releases `m`, dropping back to low priority.
4. H takes `m` and runs.

In this isolated three-thread example, H waits for L's remaining critical section plus scheduling overhead. General bounds must include nesting, higher-priority interference and any blocking by the holder. Inheritance must be **transitive**: if L is itself blocked on a lock held by another thread, that thread is boosted too.

An alternative is an **immediate priority ceiling** protocol: each mutex gets a ceiling equal to the highest priority of any thread that may lock it, and whoever holds it runs at the ceiling straight away. It needs the ceiling worked out in advance, but avoids repeated priority changes.

POSIX exposes both as mutex attributes. This configuration fragment assumes m is a declared mutex; production code must check the return values and destroy the attribute object when finished:

```c
pthread_mutexattr_t a;
pthread_mutexattr_init(&a);
pthread_mutexattr_setprotocol(
    &a, PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT);
/* or PTHREAD_PRIO_PROTECT for ceiling */
pthread_mutex_init(&m, &a);
```

On Linux, `PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT` mutexes are built on PI futexes and the kernel's `rt_mutex`, which handles chains of boosts. The PREEMPT_RT real-time kernel goes further and converts most kernel spinlocks into priority-inheriting sleeping locks for the same reason.

Priority inversion matters most for real-time threads with strict priorities. Ordinary Linux threads under the fair scheduler suffer milder versions: a low-weight thread holding a lock still runs, just slowly. The next module covers locks in depth.

## Key takeaways
- A medium-priority task can delay a high-priority waiter by preempting its low-priority lock holder.
- Priority inheritance boosts holders along blocking chains; priority ceilings use precomputed mutex ceilings.
- Pathfinder’s firsthand account describes enabling inheritance through a tested patch, without using a VxWorks shell.

## Further reading
- [Scheduling: The Multi-Level Feedback Queue — OSTEP](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/cpu-sched-mlfq.pdf)
- [Glenn Reeves: what happened on Pathfinder — firsthand correction in RISKS](https://catless.ncl.ac.uk/Risks/19.54.html)
- [Priority inversion — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Priority_inversion)
- [Priority inheritance — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Priority_inheritance)
- [RT-mutex subsystem with PI support — Linux kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/locking/rt-mutex.html)
- [Multilevel feedback queue — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multilevel_feedback_queue)

questions.prompt: One CPU, strict preemptive priorities. L (low) locks mutex `m`. H (high) wakes and blocks on `m`. M (medium, CPU-bound, never touches `m`) wakes. With **no** priority inheritance, what runs, and for how long is H delayed?

options.text: L runs until it releases `m`; H waits only for L's critical section
options.explanation: That's what priority inheritance would give you. Without it, M outranks L and preempts it.

options.text: H runs, because it has the highest priority
options.explanation: H is blocked on `m`. A blocked thread can't run regardless of priority.

options.text: M runs; H is delayed for as long as M (and any other medium work) keeps running
options.explanation: Correct. M preempts L, L can't release `m`, and H waits on M. The delay is unbounded: this is priority inversion.

options.text: The threads deadlock and nothing runs
options.explanation: There is no circular wait: M continues executing. M may finish or keep running indefinitely, so H’s unbounded delay is not a deadlock.

questions.workedExample:
Step through it:

1. H is blocked on `m`, so it's not ready.
2. Ready threads: L and M. M outranks L, so **M runs**.
3. L can't run, so `m` stays locked, so H stays blocked.
4. H's wait now depends on how long M runs, which has nothing to do with the short critical section.

```
L holds m --- preempted -----------
H blocked on m ...................
M runs runs runs runs ............
```

With priority inheritance, L would run at H's priority, M couldn't preempt it, and H would wait for L’s remaining critical section plus scheduling overhead in this isolated three-thread model.

questions.prompt: Mars Pathfinder, 1997: the spacecraft suffered repeated total resets. What was the root cause, and how was it fixed?

options.text: A deadlock between two tasks; fixed by reordering lock acquisition in a software patch
options.explanation: There was no cycle of waits. The high-priority task was delayed by a medium-priority one, which is inversion, not deadlock.

options.text: Priority inversion in a select/pipe semaphore; engineers enabled inheritance, tested the change and applied it through the spacecraft patch process
options.explanation: Reeves identifies the semaphore in VxWorks select/pipe handling. His firsthand account rejects the claim that the shell/C interpreter was used to patch it.

options.text: Cosmic-ray memory corruption; fixed by enabling error-correcting memory
options.explanation: The fault was reproduced on an identical copy of the spacecraft on the ground with tracing on, which pointed squarely at a software scheduling problem.

options.text: Starvation of the weather task; fixed by adding aging
options.explanation: The low-priority weather task was a participant, but the failure was the *high-priority* bus task missing its deadline, caused by the lock.

After reproducing the failure, engineers enabled inheritance, checked system-wide effects and used the validated onboard patch mechanism. This was not an interactive C-interpreter fix.

questions.prompt: Which statements about **priority inheritance** and **priority ceiling** are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: With inheritance, a lock holder is boosted only when a higher-priority thread actually blocks on its lock
options.explanation: Correct. Inheritance reacts to a higher-priority waiter. Releasing a lock removes its donation; a holder can retain boosts required by waiters on other locks.

options.text: Inheritance must be transitive: if the boosted holder is itself blocked on another lock, that lock's holder is boosted too
options.explanation: Correct. Otherwise a chain of locks would reintroduce the inversion one level down. Linux's rt_mutex handles such chains.

options.text: The ceiling protocol needs, in advance, the highest priority of any thread that may take the lock
options.explanation: Correct. The ceiling is computed ahead of time, and any holder runs at it immediately.

options.text: Inheritance eliminates all waiting by the high-priority thread
options.explanation: Inheritance removes the medium-priority interference in the simple example. General delay bounds also depend on nested locks, holder blocking and higher-priority work; inheritance does not eliminate waiting.

options.text: In POSIX, inheritance is chosen with PTHREAD_PRIO_PROTECT
options.explanation: PTHREAD_PRIO_PROTECT selects the ceiling protocol. Inheritance is PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT.

questions.workedExample: Options A, B and C describe inheritance, transitive inheritance and immediate priority ceilings. Option D is false: inheritance removes medium-priority interference in the simple example but H still waits for the holder; general bounds depend on nesting and other interference. Option E reverses the constants: INHERIT requests inheritance and PROTECT requests a priority ceiling.

lessons.title: Linux scheduler history and class ordering
lessons.summary: Classic scheduler names describe different selection policies across kernel versions.
lessons.body:
The earlier MLFQ units describe a policy that guesses which jobs are interactive and rewards them. Linux took a different route in 2007: stop guessing, and divide the CPU **fairly**, in proportion to a weight. That idea, the Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS), entered mainline in Linux 2.6.23. Linux 6.6, released in 2023, changed fair-class selection to **EEVDF**, which keeps weighted fairness and adds an explicit notion of latency. Deployed distributions can retain older kernels or backport changes.

Real-time work sits above all of this, in strict-priority classes that the fair scheduler never overrides.
## A short history

The O(...) labels are Big O notation, where n is the number of runnable tasks: O(n) means picking the next task took time proportional to n, and O(1) means it took the same time however many tasks there were.

| Kernel | Scheduler |
|---|---|
| 2.4 | O(n): scan runnable tasks |
| 2.6.0 (2003) | O(1): priority arrays plus interactivity heuristics |
| 2.6.23 (2007) | CFS |
| 6.6 (2023) | EEVDF replaces CFS's pick logic |
| 6.12 (2024) | sched_ext: schedulers in BPF |

The O(1) scheduler was fast but relied on heuristics to guess which tasks were interactive, much like MLFQ. Those heuristics could be fooled, and desktop latency suffered under load. Con Kolivas's fairness-based RSDL patches showed a simpler approach worked, and Ingo Molnar wrote CFS in response.
## Scheduling classes

The kernel doesn't have one scheduler; it has a stack of **scheduling classes**, checked in strict order. Ordinary selection considers higher classes first, subject to bandwidth limits. A deadline-class fair server can also dispatch fair work to prevent starvation.

```
stop      (kernel internal, per CPU)
deadline  SCHED_DEADLINE
rt        SCHED_FIFO, SCHED_RR (1-99)
fair      SCHED_NORMAL, SCHED_BATCH,
          SCHED_IDLE
ext       sched_ext (BPF, if loaded)
idle      the idle task
```

Ignoring throttling and fair-server service, an eligible `SCHED_FIFO` thread outranks normal threads regardless of nice. Ordinary applications usually use `SCHED_NORMAL` (`SCHED_OTHER` in the userspace API). A loaded sched_ext scheduler can take over normal, batch and idle-policy tasks; in partial mode it handles only `SCHED_EXT` tasks.

## Key takeaways
- Classic scheduler names describe different selection policies across kernel versions.
- Real-time and deadline classes normally outrank fair work, subject to bandwidth controls and fair-server service.
- sched_ext can replace normal scheduling according to its configured mode.

## Further reading
- [CFS Scheduler — Linux kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-design-CFS.html)
- [EEVDF Scheduler — Linux kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-eevdf.html)
- [An EEVDF CPU scheduler for Linux — LWN](https://lwn.net/Articles/925371/)
- [Completing the EEVDF scheduler — LWN](https://lwn.net/Articles/969062/)
- [Deadline Task Scheduling — Linux kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-deadline.html)
- [Real-Time group scheduling — Linux kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-rt-group.html)
- [sched(7) — Linux manual page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/sched.7.html)

options.explanation: Nice −20 is the heaviest weight *within the fair class*. It doesn't let a normal thread compete with the real-time class at all.

options.text: They share the CPU in proportion to their weights

lessons.title: CFS: compare weighted virtual clocks
lessons.summary: Classic CFS selects the task with the smallest virtual runtime.
lessons.body:
## CFS: an ideal CPU, simulated

CFS’s design starts from an imaginary ideal multi-tasking CPU. For equal-weight runnable tasks sharing one CPU, each receives an equal fraction of its service:

```formula
s = 1 / n
s = 1 / 4 = 0.25
where
s: each task’s ideal CPU share, a dimensionless fraction
n: the number of equal-weight runnable tasks, four in the example
In words: four equally weighted competitors would each receive a quarter of one CPU.
```

Different weights produce unequal shares, covered in the next unit. Real hardware can run only one task per CPU at a time, so CFS tracks how far each task has fallen behind that ideal.

The tool is **virtual runtime** (`vruntime`), in nanoseconds. Every task has a **scheduling weight** (set by its nice value, below); a normal nice 0 task has weight 1024. When a task runs, its vruntime is advanced by the real time it ran, scaled by how its weight compares with 1024:

```formula
v_new = v_old + (1024t_run) / w
v_new = 50 ms + 4 ms × 1024 / 1024
v_new = 54 ms
where
v_new: the task's vruntime after it has run, in nanoseconds (ns) inside the kernel; milliseconds (ms) in these examples
v_old: the task's vruntime before it ran, same units
t_run: the real CPU time the task just ran for, same units
w: the task's weight; 1024 for nice 0, larger for more important tasks and smaller for less important ones
ns: nanoseconds, billionths of a second
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
In words: a nice 0 task's virtual clock runs at real speed; a heavier task's runs slower and a lighter task's faster, so lighter tasks look as if they have had more CPU than they really have.
```

In the example, a nice 0 task with vruntime 50 ms runs for 4 ms and ends up at 54 ms. The formula is the whole of CFS's fairness: it holds for tasks in the fair class competing on one run queue.

The rule for picking is then trivial: **run the task with the smallest vruntime**, the one that has had least.

To find it fast, CFS keeps runnable tasks in a **red-black tree** ordered by vruntime, caching the leftmost node. Here n is the number of tasks represented in the tree. Picking is O(1); inserting a task after it runs or wakes is O(log n), time that grows with the logarithm of *n*: roughly one more step each time the number of runnable tasks doubles.

```
          [B 40]
         /      \
     [A 25]    [D 70]
     /
 [C 10] <- leftmost: runs next
```

As C runs, its vruntime rises. The current task is normally kept outside the queued-task tree, then reinserted at its new ordering position when descheduled. Classic CFS compares its service with queued competitors and applies slice/granularity and wake-up checks to decide when to reschedule; the picture shows key ordering rather than a node continuously moving through the tree.

## Key takeaways
- Classic CFS selects the task with the smallest virtual runtime.
- Virtual runtime grows faster for lighter tasks and slower for heavier tasks.
- A cached leftmost tree node makes selection constant-time; maintaining the ordered tree costs logarithmic time.

## Further reading

- [Real-Time group scheduling — Linux kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-rt-group.html)
- [sched(7) — Linux manual page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/sched.7.html)

1. CFS's rule: run the task with the **smallest vruntime**.
2. Order by increasing virtual runtime: C, A, B, then D.
3. C is leftmost, so C runs.

```
        [B 40]
       /      \
   [A 25]    [D 70]
   /
[C 10]  <- leftmost
```

As C runs its virtual runtime grows. Classic CFS uses runtime and granularity checks to decide when another task should run; the tree drawing illustrates ordering, not an exact preemption timestamp.

lessons.title: Turn nice weights into CPU shares
lessons.summary: Nice changes a task’s fair scheduling weight, not its scheduling class.
lessons.body:
## Weights and nice

Nice values map to weights through a fixed table in the kernel. Nice 0 is 1024, and each step is a factor of about **1.25**, so the table is close to this formula:

```formula
w ≈ 1024 / (1.25^n)
w ≈ 1024 / (1.25^5) ≈ 335.54
w ≈ 1024 / (1.25^{−5}) = 3125
where
w: the task's weight, a plain number with no unit
n: the task's nice value, from −20 to 19
1.25^n: 1.25 raised to the power n (a negative n gives 1 divided by 1.25 raised to the power −n)
≈: approximately equal to; the real table is rounded and differs slightly
In words: each nice step up divides the weight by about 1.25, and each step down multiplies it by about 1.25.
```

The exact kernel values:

| Nice | Weight |
|---|---|
| −20 | 88761 |
| −5 | 3121 |
| 0 | 1024 |
| 1 | 820 |
| 5 | 335 |
| 19 | 15 |

Weights turn into CPU time like this: when several tasks in one fair group all want the CPU, each gets its weight divided by the total weight of the competitors.

```formula
s_i = w_i / (w_1 + w_2 + … + w_n)
s_0 = 1024 / (1024 + 820) ≈ 0.555
s_1 = 820 / (1024 + 820) ≈ 0.445
where
s_i: the share of CPU time task i gets, as a fraction (0.555 means 55.5 %)
w_i: task i's weight, from the table
w_1, w_2, w_n: the weights of all n competing tasks
n: the number of runnable tasks competing for the CPU
…: "and so on" for every task in between
s_0, s_1: the shares of a nice 0 task (weight 1024) and a nice 1 task (weight 820) competing alone
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: each task gets a slice of the CPU proportional to its weight.
```

So for two otherwise equal competitors in one fair group, moving one from nice 0 to nice 1 changes the split from 50/50 to about 55.5/44.5. The share change depends on the competitors. A higher weight makes vruntime grow *more slowly*, so it needs more real CPU service to reach the same virtual-clock advance. This explains the larger fair share under classic CFS and EEVDF; EEVDF additionally compares eligibility and virtual deadlines.

**Worked example: who gets what?** Three CPU-bound tasks in the same fair group share one CPU: A and B at nice 0, C at nice 5.

```formula
w_tot = 1024 + 1024 + 335 = 2383
s_A = s_B = 1024 / 2383 ≈ 0.43
s_C = 335 / 2383 ≈ 0.14
v_C = 10 ms × 1024 / 335 ≈ 30.6 ms
where
w_tot: the total weight of the three tasks
s_A, s_B, s_C: the CPU shares of A, B and C, as fractions (0.43 means 43 %)
v_C: how much C's vruntime grows when it runs for 10 ms of real time
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: A and B each get about 43 % of the CPU and C about 14 %, because C's virtual clock runs about three times as fast.
```

Check with vruntime: after 10 ms of real time each, A and B gain 10 ms of vruntime, but C gains about 30.6 ms. C’s virtual runtime advances about three times as fast per unit of real execution, so its long-run CPU service is about a third of either nice 0 competitor’s. This is a service-time ratio, not a guarantee about how often dispatches occur.

Note what nice is *not*: it's not a strict priority. A nice 19 task alongside a nice 0 task still gets 15 / 1039, about 1.4%. That proportional share assumes competition within the same fair group, available CPU bandwidth and no overriding higher-class work.

## Key takeaways
- Nice changes a task’s fair scheduling weight, not its scheduling class.
- A task’s long-run share is its weight divided by the competitors’ total in the same fair group.
- The approximate geometric mapping explains the trend; the kernel uses an exact rounded weight table.

## Further reading
- [CFS Scheduler — Linux kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-design-CFS.html)
- [EEVDF Scheduler — Linux kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-eevdf.html)
- [An EEVDF CPU scheduler for Linux — LWN](https://lwn.net/Articles/925371/)
- [Completing the EEVDF scheduler — LWN](https://lwn.net/Articles/969062/)
- [Deadline Task Scheduling — Linux kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-deadline.html)
- [Real-Time group scheduling — Linux kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-rt-group.html)
- [sched(7) — Linux manual page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/sched.7.html)
- [Exact scheduler weight table — Linux 6.12 source](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/kernel/sched/core.c)

questions.prompt: Two CPU-bound tasks compete alone in the same fair group on one CPU: a nice 19 backup and a nice 0 service, with no quota or higher-class interference. What share does the backup receive?

options.text: The backup never runs while the service is busy
options.explanation: That's strict-priority thinking. Nice is a weight, so the backup still gets a small proportional share.

options.text: The backup gets about half the CPU
options.explanation: Half would mean equal weights. Nice 19's weight (15) is far smaller than nice 0's (1024).

options.text: Roughly 1–2% of the CPU
options.explanation: Correct: 15 / (1024 + 15) is about 1.44%. SCHED_IDLE offers still lower-weight background scheduling, not strict idle-only execution.

options.text: The backup is moved into the idle scheduling class
options.explanation: Nice never changes a task's class. The idle class only holds the per-CPU idle task.

questions.workedExample:
Within one fair group, each task's share is its weight divided by the total weight:

```formula
s_b = w_b / (w_s + w_b)
s_b = 15 / (1024 + 15)
s_b = 15 / 1039 ≈ 0.0144 ≈ 1.44 %
where
s_b: the backup's share of the CPU, as a fraction
w_b: the backup's weight at nice 19, 15
w_s: the service's weight at nice 0, 1024
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
%: per cent, hundredths
In words: the backup's weight is a tiny fraction of the total, so it gets a tiny but non-zero share.
```

Correct: 1024/1844 ≈ 55.5% and 820/1844 ≈ 44.5%, a gap of about 11.1 percentage points. Each share changes about 5.5 points from 50%.

options.text: About 80% / 20%

options.text: 100% / 0%, because the higher-priority task always runs

```formula
where
```

questions.prompt: A task at **nice 5** (weight 335) runs for **6 ms** of real CPU time. By how much does its vruntime increase?

options.text: 6 ms
options.explanation: That's the increase for a nice 0 task, whose weight is exactly 1024. Lighter tasks' vruntime grows faster.

options.text: About 2 ms
options.explanation: That divides instead of multiplying: it would be the increase for a task *heavier* than nice 0 (weight ≈ 3072).

options.text: About 18.3 ms
options.explanation: Correct. Scale the 6 ms of real service by the reference weight 1024 divided by 335; the virtual increment is about 18.3 ms.

options.text: 335 ms
options.explanation: The weight is a scaling factor, not a time: the increase is 6 ms × 1024 / 335.

questions.workedExample:
1. vruntime grows by the real time run, scaled by 1024 over the task's weight:

```formula
v_add = (1024t_run) / w
v_add = 6 ms × 1024 / 335
v_add = 6144 ms / 335 ≈ 18.3 ms
where
v_add: how much the task's vruntime grows, in milliseconds (ms)
t_run: the real CPU time it ran, 6 ms
w: the task's weight, 335 at nice 5 (1024 at nice 0)
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
In words: a task lighter than nice 0 has a virtual clock that runs faster than real time, here about three times faster.
```

2. Compare a nice 0 task: 6 ms × 1024 / 1024 = 6 ms.

Since CFS runs whichever task has the smallest vruntime, the nice 5 task drifts rightwards in the tree about 3× faster and receives roughly a third as much CPU service as a nice 0 competitor under sustained same-group contention; this does not specify dispatch counts.

lessons.title: Classic CFS sleeper placement and slices
lessons.summary: Classic CFS bounds a returning sleeper’s credit rather than replaying all missed service.
lessons.body:
## Sleepers and new tasks

A task that sleeps for a minute would wake with a tiny vruntime and monopolise the CPU while it "caught up". CFS prevents this with `min_vruntime`, a monotonic floor tracking the smallest vruntime in the queue. A waking task's vruntime is raised to roughly `min_vruntime` minus a small bonus (half a latency period), so interactive tasks get a modest head start, not a minute's worth:

```formula
v_wake = max(v_old, v_min − L / 2)
where
v_wake: the sleeper's vruntime when it wakes, in milliseconds (ms) here (nanoseconds in the kernel)
max(a, b): the larger of the two values a and b
v_old: the vruntime the task had when it went to sleep
v_min: min_vruntime, the smallest vruntime in the run queue (it only ever increases)
L: the classic CFS target latency, in milliseconds (ms); 24 ms with default logarithmic scaling at eight or more online CPUs
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
In words: a task that slept briefly keeps its own vruntime; one that slept a long time is moved up to half a target latency below the queue's minimum vruntime, so it gets a small head start and nothing more.
```

This was classic CFS behaviour, in kernels before 6.6, with its default `GENTLE_FAIR_SLEEPERS` setting, which halves the bonus (without it the bonus was a whole target latency). EEVDF, from 6.6, handles sleepers through lag instead. New tasks start near `min_vruntime` too.
## Latency and slices

CFS had no fixed quantum. It aimed to run every runnable task once within a **target latency**, with a **minimum slice** so that hundreds of tasks wouldn't each get microseconds. Both defaults grow a little on machines with more CPUs, because more CPUs share the load:

```formula
k = 1 + ⌊log_2(min(N_cpu, 8))⌋
L = 6 ms × k
g = 0.75 ms × k
k = 1 + ⌊log_2(8)⌋ = 1 + 3 = 4
L = 24 ms,  g = 3 ms
where
k: the scaling factor, from 1 (one CPU) to 4 (8 or more CPUs)
⌊x⌋: floor: round x down to a whole number
log_2(x): the base-2 logarithm of x, the power you raise 2 to in order to get x (log_2(8) = 3)
min(a, b): the smaller of the two values a and b
N_cpu: the number of CPUs online; counting stops at 8
L: the target latency, in milliseconds (ms)
g: the minimum slice (sched_min_granularity), in ms
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
In words: start from 6 ms and 0.75 ms and multiply both by a factor that grows by one each time the CPU count doubles, up to 8 CPUs.
```

On a 4-CPU machine, for example, the factor is 3, giving 18 ms and 2.25 ms.

That worked, but latency was a side effect of fairness. There was no way to say "this task wants short, frequent slices", so CFS grew wake-up heuristics to keep desktops snappy, and these were hard to reason about.

## Key takeaways
- Classic CFS bounds a returning sleeper’s credit rather than replaying all missed service.
- Target latency and minimum granularity were scaled CFS tunables, not universal application latency guarantees.
- The historical CFS sleeper rule differs from EEVDF lag handling.

## Further reading
- [CFS Scheduler — Linux kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-design-CFS.html)
- [EEVDF Scheduler — Linux kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-eevdf.html)
- [An EEVDF CPU scheduler for Linux — LWN](https://lwn.net/Articles/925371/)
- [Completing the EEVDF scheduler — LWN](https://lwn.net/Articles/969062/)
- [Deadline Task Scheduling — Linux kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-deadline.html)
- [Real-Time group scheduling — Linux kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-rt-group.html)
- [sched(7) — Linux manual page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/sched.7.html)
- [Classic CFS placement and tunables — Linux 6.5 source](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.5/kernel/sched/fair.c)

questions.prompt: In the stated classic CFS model, a long-sleeping task has virtual runtime 10 ms. The queue minimum has reached 100 ms and the target latency is 24 ms. With GENTLE_FAIR_SLEEPERS, where is its virtual runtime placed on waking?

options.text: 10 ms
options.explanation: That would preserve an enormous catch-up credit for the long sleep; the model caps the credit.

options.text: 88 ms
options.explanation: Correct. Half the target latency is 12 ms, so the floor is 88 ms, larger than the old 10 ms.

options.text: 100 ms
options.explanation: That removes the entire historical sleeper bonus rather than allowing half a target latency.

options.text: 112 ms
options.explanation: That adds the bonus in the wrong direction and places the sleeper ahead in virtual service.

Use the historical placement model, not EEVDF lag handling:

```formula

v_wake = max(10 ms, 100 ms − 12 ms)
v_wake = 88 ms
where
v_wake: waking task’s virtual runtime, in milliseconds (ms)
v_old: its old virtual runtime, 10 ms
v_min: the queue minimum virtual runtime, 100 ms
L: target latency in this stated model, 24 ms
max(a, b): choose the larger of a and b
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
In words: cap the sleeper’s head start at half the target latency rather than repaying its whole absence.
```

The calculation describes classic CFS with the stated feature setting; EEVDF handles sleepers differently.

lessons.title: EEVDF: eligibility before virtual deadline
lessons.summary: Eligibility excludes tasks already ahead of their fair service.
lessons.body:
## EEVDF: fairness plus deadlines

**Earliest Eligible Virtual Deadline First** comes from a 1995 paper by Ion Stoica and Hussein Abdel-Wahab. Peter Zijlstra's implementation became the fair-class scheduler in Linux 6.6. Weights, nice and the red-black tree stay; the *picking rule* changes.

The following equations explain an idealised single-run-queue model. Actual kernels also apply feature settings, clamping, preemption protection and hierarchical group accounting.

Two ideas:

1. **Lag.** Compare the service a task should have received on the ideal CPU with what it actually got. Positive lag means it is owed CPU; negative means it has had more than its share. In practice the kernel computes the weighted average vruntime of the queue, and a task is **eligible** if its vruntime is no more than that average (lag of zero or more):

```formula
V = (w_1 v_1 + … + w_n v_n) / W
W = w_1 + … + w_n
lag_i = w_i(V − v_i)
lag_i ≥ 0  when  v_i ≤ V
where
V: the weighted average vruntime of the run queue, in nanoseconds (ns)
w_1, w_n, w_i: the weights of the tasks, from their nice values
v_1, v_n, v_i: the vruntimes of the tasks, in ns
n: the number of runnable tasks in the queue
…: "and so on" for every task in between
W: the total weight of the queue
lag_i: a weight-scaled service-lag measure, in weight-scaled nanoseconds; its sign indicates owed service or over-service. With the reference weight 1024 used for these virtual clocks, divide this measure by 1024 to express service in real CPU-time nanoseconds
ns: nanoseconds, billionths of a second
≥, ≤: greater than or equal to, less than or equal to
In words: a task whose vruntime is at or behind the queue's average has had no more than its fair share, so it may be picked.
```

2. **Virtual deadline.** Each task requests a slice (by default the base slice). Its deadline is its vruntime plus that slice scaled by weight:

```formula
d_i = v_i + (1024r_i) / w_i
where
d_i: task i's virtual deadline, in nanoseconds (ns)
v_i: task i's vruntime, in ns
r_i: the slice task i asks for, in ns
w_i: task i's weight; 1024 for nice 0
ns: nanoseconds, billionths of a second
In words: a task's deadline is where its vruntime would be after one full slice; a shorter slice puts that deadline earlier.
```

The rule: **among eligible tasks, run the one with the earliest virtual deadline.**

Eligibility keeps it fair: nobody who is ahead of their share gets picked. Deadlines add latency control: a task asking for a **shorter slice** gets an earlier deadline, so it runs sooner, though in smaller pieces. Over time it gets the same total share.

**Worked example: short slice, same weight.** A and B are both nice 0 (weight 1024) with vruntime 0. A uses a 3 ms slice; B asks for 1 ms. Both are eligible, because both vruntimes equal the average, 0.

```formula
d_A = 0 ms + 3 ms × 1024 / 1024
d_A = 3 ms
d_B = 0 ms + 1 ms × 1024 / 1024
d_B = 1 ms
v_B = 0 ms + 1 ms = 1 ms
d_B = 1 ms + 1 ms = 2 ms
where
d_A, d_B: the virtual deadlines of A and B, in milliseconds (ms)
v_B: B's vruntime after it has run for 1 ms
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
In words: B's deadline is earlier, so B runs first, for 1 ms; its next deadline is then 2 ms.
```

B now waits for A to catch up before it is eligible again, so neither gets more than its half. B simply gets its half in smaller, more frequent pieces.

In the checked Linux 6.12 source the unscaled base slice is 0.75 ms; the default logarithmic scaling gives 3 ms at eight or more CPUs. Tunables and later kernels can differ. Since Linux 6.12 a normal task can request its own slice, between 0.1 ms and 100 ms, through the `sched_runtime` field of `sched_setattr()`.

Lag also needs care for sleepers. A task that sleeps with negative lag shouldn't wipe out its debt by sleeping briefly. Linux 6.12 introduced deferred dequeue: an over-served sleeping task can remain represented on the run queue in a "deferred dequeue" state so its lag decays, rather than simply resetting it.

> [!note] Is CFS gone?
> The name lingers: the fair class still lives in `kernel/sched/fair.c`, and many docs and tools still say CFS. Weights, nice, vruntime, group scheduling and CFS bandwidth control all carried over. What changed is how the next task is chosen and how preemption is decided.

## Key takeaways
- Eligibility excludes tasks already ahead of their fair service.
- Among eligible tasks, the earliest virtual deadline wins; a shorter requested slice changes service timing.
- Virtual deadlines are fairness coordinates, not application wall-clock deadlines; weight still controls long-run share.

## Further reading
- [CFS Scheduler — Linux kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-design-CFS.html)
- [EEVDF Scheduler — Linux kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-eevdf.html)
- [An EEVDF CPU scheduler for Linux — LWN](https://lwn.net/Articles/925371/)
- [Completing the EEVDF scheduler — LWN](https://lwn.net/Articles/969062/)
- [Deadline Task Scheduling — Linux kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-deadline.html)
- [Real-Time group scheduling — Linux kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-rt-group.html)
- [sched(7) — Linux manual page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/sched.7.html)
- [EEVDF selection and lag — Linux 6.12 source](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/v6.12/kernel/sched/fair.c)

An idealised EEVDF example has three nice 0 tasks (equal weight). All table times are milliseconds. Each starts a fresh request; ignore current-slice protection and preemption granularity. The average virtual runtime is 10 ms:

| Task | vruntime | slice |
|---|---|---|
| A | 8 | 3 |
| B | 12 | 0.5 |
| C | 10 | 0.5 |

Which task does EEVDF pick? (Classic CFS would have picked A.)

options.text: A, because it has the smallest vruntime
options.explanation: That's CFS's rule. EEVDF picks by earliest virtual deadline among eligible tasks, and A's deadline (11) is later than C's.

options.text: B, because it has the earliest deadline overall
options.explanation: B's deadline (12.5) isn't the earliest, and in any case B is not eligible: its vruntime (12) is above the average (10), so it has had more than its share.

options.text: C, because it is eligible (vruntime not above the average of 10) and has the earliest virtual deadline (10.5)
options.explanation: Correct. Eligible tasks are A (deadline 11) and C (deadline 10.5). C's short slice gives it the earlier deadline.

options.text: Whichever task woke most recently
options.explanation: Wake-up order isn't the selection criterion. Wake-ups trigger a preemption check, but the pick is by eligibility and deadline.

questions.workedExample:
1. **Eligibility**: a task may be picked only if its vruntime is not above the queue's average.

```formula
V = 10 ms
v_A = 8 ms ≤ V
v_B = 12 ms > V
v_C = 10 ms ≤ V
where
V: the weighted average vruntime of the queue (all weights are equal here, so it is the plain average)
v_A, v_B, v_C: the vruntimes of A, B and C, in milliseconds (ms)
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
≤: less than or equal to
>: greater than
In words: A and C are at or behind the average, so they are owed CPU; B is ahead of its share and must wait.
```

2. **Deadlines** (equal nice 0 weights, so the slice is not rescaled):

```formula
d = v + (1024r) / w
d_A = 8 ms + 3 ms = 11 ms
d_C = 10 ms + 0.5 ms = 10.5 ms
where
d: a task’s virtual deadline, in milliseconds (ms)
v: the task’s virtual runtime, in ms
r: its requested slice, in ms
w: the task's weight, 1024 at nice 0
d_A, d_C: the deadlines of the eligible tasks A and C, in ms
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
In words: each deadline is where the task's vruntime would be after one slice; C's short slice puts its deadline first.
```

3. Earliest eligible deadline: **C**.

C hasn't had less CPU than A, but by asking for short slices it gets served sooner. It will just get its share in smaller pieces, so fairness is preserved.

questions.prompt: On Linux 6.12+, a latency-sensitive nice 0 audio thread uses `sched_setattr()` to request a **1 ms** slice instead of the default (about 3 ms on this machine). A CPU-bound nice 0 thread shares its CPU. Which effects should you expect? Select all that apply.

options.text: The audio thread's virtual deadlines are earlier, so it tends to be picked sooner when it becomes eligible
options.explanation: Correct. The virtual deadline is the vruntime plus the requested slice scaled by weight, so a smaller slice gives an earlier deadline.

options.text: The audio thread now gets a larger long-run share of the CPU
options.explanation: Share is set by weight, and both are nice 0. A short slice changes *when* and *in what size pieces* it runs, not how much in total.

options.text: The audio thread runs in smaller pieces, so there may be more context switches
options.explanation: Correct. Shorter slices mean more frequent switching, the usual latency-versus-overhead trade-off.

options.text: The audio thread moves into the real-time class
options.explanation: A custom slice keeps the task in the fair class. Only an RT or deadline policy moves it to a higher class.

questions.workedExample:
Weight sets long-run share under same-group sustained contention; equal nice weights receive equal shares when no other constraints intervene. A slice affects virtual deadlines. For fresh requests at equal virtual runtimes:

```formula
d = v + (1024r) / w
d_audio = v + 1 ms
d_hog = v + 3 ms
where
d: a fresh request's virtual deadline, in milliseconds (ms)
v: its starting virtual runtime, in ms; equal for these two requests
r: its requested slice, in ms
w: its weight, 1024 for both nice 0 tasks
d_audio, d_hog: deadlines of the fresh audio and CPU-heavy requests, in ms
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
In words: at equal starting virtual runtimes the shorter fresh request has the earlier virtual deadline.
```

The audio request therefore has the earlier deadline in that comparison. At later selections, virtual runtimes, eligibility, request progress and preemption protection can differ; an arbitrary audio deadline is not always earlier. A shorter slice does not guarantee a wall-clock latency or change the scheduling class.

lessons.title: Fairness between groups and scheduler inspection
lessons.summary: Thread-level nice acts within a scheduling group; group weights control competition between groups.
lessons.body:
## Fairness between whom?

Linux schedules **threads**, not processes. Within one fair group, equal-weight runnable threads compete individually: sixteen such threads collectively receive sixteen shares against one for a single-threaded competitor, when CPU capacity is contested. Two mechanisms rebalance this:

- **Group scheduling**: with cgroups, the fair scheduler first divides CPU between groups (by `cpu.weight` in cgroup v2, default 100), then between tasks within a group. systemd commonly organises services and user sessions into cgroups; the actual hierarchy and enabled controllers determine the competing groups.
- **Autogroup** (since 2.6.38): on kernels with it enabled, each terminal session gets its own group, so a `make -j32` in one terminal doesn't swamp your desktop.

One surprise follows: under group scheduling, a thread's nice value only matters **relative to other threads in the same group**. When two autogroups compete and a task is alone in its group, renicing that task changes no relative competitor inside that group. Different cgroup layouts or other tasks within the groups can change the outcome.
## The other fair policies

- **SCHED_BATCH**: fair share, but treated as CPU-bound and preempts others less; good for batch jobs that want cache-friendly long runs.
- **SCHED_IDLE**: extremely low-weight background work in the fair class. It is not the per-CPU idle task and does not promise zero service whenever normal work is runnable.
## Seeing it on a real system

The following ps listing is illustrative; policies, identifiers and commands on your host will differ.

```
$ ps -eLo pid,tid,cls,rtprio,ni,comm
  PID   TID CLS RTPRIO  NI COMMAND
  612   612  TS      -   0 sshd
  880   901  FF     50   - audio-engine
 1200  1200  TS      -  19 backup
```

`TS` is the fair class, `FF` is FIFO, `RR` is round robin, `DLN` is deadline. In `top`, the PR column shows 20 plus the nice value for normal tasks; real-time tasks show negative numbers (minus 1 minus their real-time priority), and `rt` for real-time priority 99.

`/proc/<pid>/sched` shows a task's vruntime, slice and switch counts, and `perf sched` records scheduling latency. Several fair-scheduler debugging tunables moved from /proc/sys/kernel to /sys/kernel/debug/sched/ in Linux 5.13. Other settings, including RT bandwidth and RR timeslice controls, remain sysctls; availability also depends on configuration and privileges.
## Pitfalls

- **Expecting nice to be a priority.** It's a weight. Nice 19 gets a small fair share; `SCHED_IDLE` gives background work an even smaller weight, not a strict idle-only guarantee.
- **Renicing across groups.** With autogroup or cgroups, nice only competes within the group. Use `cpu.weight` between groups.
- **Making things real-time "to be safe".** An RT thread that spins starves everything below it, including kernel threads that it may depend on. Use RT for short, bounded work.
- **RT with ordinary locks.** RT threads sharing locks with normal threads invite priority inversion; use `PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT` mutexes.

## Key takeaways
- Thread-level nice acts within a scheduling group; group weights control competition between groups.
- SCHED_IDLE remains a low-weight fair policy, separate from the per-CPU idle task.
- Inspect per-thread policies and queue behaviour before changing tunables or selecting real-time policies.

options.text: About 6% (1/17), then 50%
options.explanation: Correct. Linux schedules threads, so in one group Q gets 1 of 17 equal shares. With separate equal-weight groups, CPU is split 50/50 between groups first.
Process-level fairness only happens when processes are in separate groups. Within one group, each thread is an equal competitor.

options.text: About 6% (1/17) in both cases
options.explanation: Separate groups change the first level of division: groups share by weight before threads share within a group.

options.text: Nearly 0%, then about 6%
options.explanation: Fair scheduling never starves a nice 0 thread. And with equal-weight groups Q gets half, not 1/17.

questions.workedExample:
**Same group**: the fair scheduler sees 17 equal-weight threads.

```formula
s_Q = 1 / 17 ≈ 0.059 ≈ 5.9 %
s_P = 16 / 17 ≈ 0.94 ≈ 94 %
where
s_Q: Q's share of the CPU (one of 17 equal shares)
s_P: P's share (16 of 17 equal shares)
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
%: per cent, hundredths
In words: with equal weights, CPU is split by counting threads.
```

**Separate groups, equal weight**: CPU is first divided between groups, then within each.

```formula
s_grp = 1 / 2 = 50 %
s_t = 50 % / 16 ≈ 3.1 %
where
s_grp: each group's share (two groups, equal weight)
s_t: the share of each of P's 16 threads
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
%: per cent, hundredths
In words: the groups split the CPU in half first; Q's single thread keeps all of its half, while P's half is cut 16 ways.
```

This is why systemd puts services in their own cgroups and why autogroup exists: so that thread count doesn't decide who gets the CPU.

lessons.title: Real-time priorities and deadline admission
lessons.summary: FIFO has no quantum; RR rotates tasks only within equal RT priorities.
lessons.body:
## Real-time classes

For audio, industrial control and low-latency trading, fairness is the wrong goal. The `rt` class gives **strict priorities** from 1 to 99 (higher wins):

- **SCHED_FIFO**: runs until it blocks, yields or is preempted by a higher RT priority. No time slice at all.
- **SCHED_RR**: the same, but threads at *equal* priority rotate with a time slice (100 ms by default, `sched_rr_timeslice_ms`).

```python
import os

# Needs CAP_SYS_NICE or
# sufficient RLIMIT_RTPRIO
os.sched_setscheduler(
    0, os.SCHED_FIFO, os.sched_param(50))

# Confirm this thread’s policy if permitted.
print(os.sched_getscheduler(0)
      == os.SCHED_FIFO)  # True on success
```

From the shell: `chrt -f 50 ./audio-engine`, and `chrt -p <pid>` to inspect.

> [!warning] A runaway FIFO thread
> A `SCHED_FIFO` thread stuck in a busy loop never yields, so nothing below it runs on that CPU: not your shell, not `kill`. Linux guards against this. RT throttling commonly limits RT work to 950 ms per 1 s (`sched_rt_runtime_us` / `sched_rt_period_us`). Linux 6.12 also introduced a deadline-class fair server that can supply CPU to fair tasks. These are distinct mechanisms; behaviour depends on kernel version, configuration and tunables.
## SCHED_DEADLINE

Since Linux 3.14, the top policy is **SCHED_DEADLINE**. Instead of a priority, a task declares three numbers:

- **Runtime parameter**: CPU time budget for the reservation per period;
- **Deadline parameter**: by when the job should finish, relative to its release;
- **Period parameter**: the reservation’s nominal repeating interval.

```
chrt -d --sched-runtime  5000000 \
        --sched-deadline 10000000 \
        --sched-period  16666666 0 ./render
```

That says "5 ms of CPU every 16.7 ms frame, finished within 10 ms". The kernel schedules deadline tasks by **Earliest Deadline First**, and uses the Constant Bandwidth Server to stop any task exceeding its runtime. It also performs **admission control**. Each task's **utilisation** is the fraction of one CPU it reserves, and the kernel refuses a new task if the total would go over the permitted limit:

```formula
U = t_run / T
U = 5 ms / 16.7 ms ≈ 0.30
U_1 + U_2 + … + U_n ≤ 0.95M
where
U: one task's utilisation, the fraction of a CPU it reserves (0.30 means 30 %)
t_run: the task's runtime per period, in milliseconds (ms)
T: the task's period, in ms
U_1, U_2, U_n: the utilisations of all n deadline tasks, including the new one
n: the number of deadline tasks
…: "and so on"
M: the number of CPUs in the group of CPUs being checked (its root domain); on chips mixing big and little cores the kernel sums the CPUs' relative capacities instead
0.95: the default limit per CPU, from sched_rt_runtime_us / sched_rt_period_us = 950000 / 1000000
≤: less than or equal to
≈: approximately equal to
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
In words: the render task reserves about 30 % of a CPU, and all deadline tasks together may reserve at most 95 % of each CPU by default.
```

If the new task does not fit, `sched_setattr()` fails with `EBUSY`. From Linux 6.12 the fair server described above is itself a deadline reservation (by default 50 ms in every 1 s, 5 % of each CPU) counted in the same total, so in the checked 6.12 source ordinary deadline tasks can reserve only about 90 % of each CPU unless the fair server is reconfigured. Admission checks reserve bandwidth; acceptance alone is not a universal proof that application deadlines will be met. Worst-case execution time, blocking, deadline versus period, CPU topology and scheduling assumptions still matter. The kernel documentation distinguishes schedulability tests from the simpler utilization admission test.

## Key takeaways
- FIFO has no quantum; RR rotates tasks only within equal RT priorities.
- Deadline scheduling reserves runtime, deadline and period parameters and rejects excess bandwidth reservations.
- Admission alone is not a proof of all application deadlines; blocking, execution bounds and topology still matter.

## Further reading
