- [EEVDF Scheduler — Linux kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-eevdf.html)
- [An EEVDF CPU scheduler for Linux — LWN](https://lwn.net/Articles/925371/)
- [Completing the EEVDF scheduler — LWN](https://lwn.net/Articles/969062/)
- [Deadline Task Scheduling — Linux kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-deadline.html)
- [Real-Time group scheduling — Linux kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-rt-group.html)
- [sched(7) — Linux manual page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/sched.7.html)

questions.prompt: Which statements about Linux's `SCHED_FIFO` and `SCHED_RR` are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Real-time priorities run from 1 to 99, and a higher number wins
options.explanation: Correct. Unlike nice, RT priorities are 'higher is higher'.

options.text: Ignoring throttling and higher scheduling classes, FIFO has no time slice and runs until blocking, yielding or higher RT priority preemption
options.explanation: Correct. FIFO has no time slice at all.

options.text: SCHED_RR threads rotate with a time slice only among threads of the same priority
options.explanation: Correct. A higher-priority RR thread still preempts immediately; the slice (100 ms by default) only matters for ties.

options.text: A SCHED_RR thread that uses its slice drops to the fair class
options.explanation: RR threads are never demoted out of the rt class. They go to the back of the queue for their own priority.

options.text: Any user can set SCHED_FIFO on their own processes
options.explanation: It needs root, CAP_SYS_NICE, or a suitable RLIMIT_RTPRIO, because an RT thread can starve the whole system.

questions.workedExample: Options A, B and C are true under the stated exclusions. RT priority is 1–99; FIFO has no quantum; RR rotates equals. RR does not demote into fair scheduling. Option E is false: setting FIFO requires CAP_SYS_NICE or suitable RLIMIT_RTPRIO permissions, not merely ownership.

questions.prompt: A single-CPU system allows deadline tasks up to **95%** of the CPU. Two `SCHED_DEADLINE` tasks already run: 30 ms per 100 ms, and 40 ms per 100 ms. A third asks for **runtime 12 ms, period 40 ms**. What happens?

options.text: It's accepted and all three tasks will occasionally miss deadlines
options.explanation: SCHED_DEADLINE's point is that it doesn't overcommit. It checks before accepting.

options.text: sched_setattr() fails with EBUSY because total utilisation would be 100%, over the 95% limit
options.explanation: Correct. 0.30 + 0.40 + 0.30 = 1.00 > 0.95, so admission control rejects the new task up front.

options.text: It's accepted at a lower real-time priority
options.explanation: Deadline tasks don't have priorities to fall back on. Either the reservation fits or it is refused.

options.text: It's accepted, and the kernel shortens its runtime to fit
options.explanation: The kernel doesn't silently change a task's parameters. It returns an error so the caller can decide.

questions.workedExample:
Each task's utilisation is its runtime divided by its period. Add them up and compare with the limit:

```formula
U = t_run / T
U_tot = (30 ms / 100 ms)
      + (40 ms / 100 ms)
      + (12 ms / 40 ms)
U_tot = 0.30 + 0.40 + 0.30 = 1.00
U_tot = 1.00 > U_max = 0.95
where
U: one task's utilisation, the fraction of the CPU it reserves
t_run: the task's runtime per period, in milliseconds (ms)
T: the task's period, in ms
U_tot: the total utilisation if the new task were accepted
U_max: the admission limit on this one-CPU system, 0.95
>: greater than
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
In words: the three reservations together would need the whole CPU, more than the 95 % allowed, so the new one is refused.
```

The request is rejected with EBUSY, assuming otherwise valid parameters and permissions. A request of 10 ms per 40 ms (0.25) makes the total exactly 0.95 and passes this bandwidth check. Passing admission does not alone prove all application deadlines will be met.

lessons.title: Hardware topology, cache affinity and run queues
lessons.summary: Logical CPUs can share core resources and caches, so thread count is not physical-core capacity.
lessons.body:
Everything so far assumed one CPU. Servers may expose many logical CPUs, arranged in hardware-dependent hierarchies of SMT threads, cores, caches and memory nodes. The scheduler now answers two questions: *which* thread runs next, and *where*. Getting "where" wrong costs cache misses, remote memory accesses, and, inside containers, whole periods of enforced idleness.
## The hardware the scheduler sees

```
Socket / NUMA node 0        node 1
+-----------------------+   +-------
| L3 (shared)           |   | L3 ...
| core0     core1  ...  |   |
| [t0 t1]   [t2 t3]     |   |
| L1/L2     L1/L2       |   |
+--------local DRAM-----+   +-------
```

- **SMT siblings** (hyper-threads) share one core's execution units and L1/L2 caches. Resource contention can make two busy siblings slower than using separate physical cores; the effect depends on the workloads.
- **Cores in one CPU socket** may form several cache-sharing groups, especially across chiplets. Many designs share an L3 within a group; the exact layout is hardware-specific.
- **NUMA nodes** each have their own memory. Reaching another node's memory goes over an interconnect and is slower.

A thread that has been running on a CPU has a **warm cache** there: its working set is in L1, L2 and L3. Move it, and it pays to reload that state. This is **cache affinity**, and it is the central tension of multicore scheduling: keep threads where their data is, but don't leave CPUs idle while work waits elsewhere.
## One queue or many?

OSTEP frames the two basic designs:

| Design | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| Single shared queue | Simple, balanced by construction | Lock contention, poor affinity |
| Per-CPU queues | Scalable, natural affinity | Load imbalance |

In a simple global-queue design, scheduling decisions contend for one lock and may move tasks between CPUs. The scaling limit and cache cost depend on implementation and workload; a global queue can also incorporate affinity heuristics.

With **per-CPU run queues**, each CPU normally uses its own queue lock rather than one lock shared by every CPU, and threads tend to stay put. The cost is **load imbalance**: CPU 0 might have four runnable threads while CPU 1 is idle. The fix is **task migration**, moving threads between queues, typically by **work stealing**: an idle or lightly loaded CPU pulls work from a busier one.

Linux has used per-CPU run queues since the O(1) scheduler in 2.6.0. Go's runtime, Java's ForkJoinPool and Tokio use the same per-worker-queue-plus-stealing idea in user space.

## Key takeaways
- Logical CPUs can share core resources and caches, so thread count is not physical-core capacity.
- Per-CPU queues reduce shared contention and preserve locality but can become imbalanced.
- Migration balances work at the cost of moving away from warm data.

## Further reading
- [Multiprocessor Scheduling (Advanced) — OSTEP](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/cpu-sched-multi.pdf)
- [Scheduler Domains — Linux kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-domains.html)
- [CFS Bandwidth Control — Linux kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-bwc.html)
- [Control Group v2 — Linux kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html)
- [sched_setaffinity(2) — Linux manual page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/sched_setaffinity.2.html)
- [numa(7) — Linux manual page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/numa.7.html)
- [Non-uniform memory access — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-uniform_memory_access)

questions.prompt: Why does Linux give each CPU its own run queue instead of sharing one global queue?

options.text: A global queue can't support priorities
options.explanation: A single queue can hold priorities perfectly well. The problems are contention and affinity, not expressiveness.

options.text: Per-CPU queues guarantee perfect load balance
options.explanation: It's the opposite: per-CPU queues can become imbalanced, which is why Linux needs migration and CPU load balancing.

options.text: Per-CPU queues avoid a single lock contended by every CPU, and keep threads on the CPU where their cache is warm
options.explanation: Correct. Scalability and cache affinity are the two wins. The cost is imbalance, which the CPU load balancer fixes.

options.text: Each CPU runs a different scheduling algorithm
options.explanation: Every CPU runs the same scheduling classes. Only the queue of tasks differs.

questions.workedExample:
Compare the two designs:

| | Global queue | Per-CPU queues |
|---|---|---|
| Locking | One lock for all CPUs | Mostly local |
| Affinity | Threads hop CPUs | Threads stay put |
| Balance | Automatic | Needs migration |

On a many-core machine, a single scheduling lock can become contended and migrations can discard useful locality; the actual cost depends on implementation and workload. A global queue can also use affinity heuristics. So Linux uses per-CPU queues and pays for it with a CPU load balancer.

questions.prompt: A machine has 4 physical cores with 2 hyper-threads each (CPUs 0–7, where 0/1, 2/3, 4/5 and 6/7 are siblings). You pin two CPU-bound, cache-heavy threads with `taskset -c 0,1`. The rest of the machine is idle. Compared with letting the scheduler place them, what do you expect?

options.text: Same throughput, since each thread has its own logical CPU
options.explanation: Distinct logical-CPU identifiers do not imply separate physical cores. Sharing core resources can constrain throughput compared with independent cores; the effect needs measurement.

options.text: Better throughput, because the threads share an L1 cache
options.explanation: Sharing a cache can help data-sharing workloads, but separate cache-heavy working sets can contend; sharing is not a general throughput guarantee.

options.text: The scheduler will move one thread to another core to fix the imbalance
options.explanation: A hard affinity mask is never overridden by the CPU load balancer. It can only choose within CPUs 0 and 1.

options.text: Usually lower throughput for this contending workload: both are restricted to one core while separate cores are idle
options.explanation: The mask prevents spreading onto physical cores. This creates a plausible resource bottleneck, rather than a universal measured speed ratio; verify on the actual CPU and workload.

questions.workedExample:
1. CPUs 0 and 1 are **SMT siblings**: one core, shared execution units and L1/L2.
2. Two CPU-bound threads there each get only part of that core.
3. Unpinned, the balancer would see 3 idle physical cores and spread the threads onto separate cores.
4. The affinity mask forbids that, so the kernel can't fix it.

Lesson: if you pin, pin to **different cores** (e.g. `taskset -c 0,2`), and know your topology (`lscpu -e`).

lessons.title: Balance load or constrain placement with affinity
lessons.summary: Scheduling domains represent hardware locality and guide balancing.
lessons.body:
## How Linux balances load

Linux describes the topology as nested **scheduling domains**, built at boot:

```
NUMA   : node0 <---------> node1
MC(LLC): [c0 c1 c2 c3]   [c4 c5 c6 c7]
SMT    : [t0 t1] [t2 t3] ...
```

Balancing happens at each level, more often and more eagerly at the bottom, where moving a thread is cheap (siblings share caches), and less often at the top, where it is expensive (crossing NUMA nodes loses cache *and* memory locality).

Three triggers drive it:

1. **Periodic balancing**: from the scheduler tick, each CPU checks whether its domain is imbalanced and pulls tasks if so. Intervals grow with domain level.
2. **Idle balancing**: a CPU that is about to go idle first tries to pull a task from a busier CPU ("newidle" balancing).
3. **Wake-up placement**: when a thread wakes, the kernel chooses a CPU for it. It prefers the previous CPU (warm cache), or an idle CPU sharing the same last-level cache, and considers placing a wakee near its waker.

The balancer also avoids moving a task that ran very recently, treating it as **cache-hot** (the default threshold, `sched_migration_cost`, is 0.5 ms). Balancing considers several signals, including runnable task counts and PELT averages. PELT tracks load, runnable time and running utilization separately; weighted load and CPU utilization are not interchangeable.

> [!note] SMT is treated specially
> Two busy threads on sibling hyper-threads of one core, while another core sits idle, is a bad placement. Linux's balancer prefers spreading busy work across physical cores first, and only then doubling up on siblings.
## CPU affinity: pinning threads

Sometimes you know better than the balancer. **Affinity** restricts which CPUs a thread may run on. The following output is illustrative for an eight-CPU Linux environment where CPUs 2 and 3 are allowed; identifiers and masks differ on other hosts.

```python
import os

print(os.sched_getaffinity(0))
# {0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7}


# Replace this thread's allowed CPU mask.
os.sched_setaffinity(0, {2, 3})
print(os.sched_getaffinity(0))
# {2, 3}
```

From the shell: `taskset -c 2,3 ./server`, or `taskset -cp <pid>` to inspect. In C, `sched_setaffinity()` or `pthread_setaffinity_np()` per thread. Affinity is inherited across `fork()`.

Layers of control, from soft to hard:

- **Default (soft affinity)**: the scheduler prefers the last CPU but migrates freely.
- **`sched_setaffinity` / `taskset`**: a hard mask per thread.
- **cpuset cgroups** (`cpuset.cpus`, `cpuset.mems`): a mask for a whole group, which processes inside cannot widen. Kubernetes's static CPU manager can give eligible Guaranteed containers with integer CPU requests exclusive logical CPUs. Whole-core allocation additionally depends on policy options such as `full-pcpus-only`.
- **`isolcpus=` / `nohz_full=` boot options**: selected isolcpus modes can exclude CPUs from general domain balancing; nohz_full can suppress periodic ticks when its conditions are met. Neither option alone removes every interrupt, kernel task or housekeeping activity. Used for packet processing, HFT and real-time control.

When pinning helps:

- Latency-critical threads that must never share a core (with the rest of the system kept off those CPUs).
- Keeping a thread on the same NUMA node as its memory or NIC interrupts.
- Benchmarks, where migrations add noise.

When it hurts:

- Pinning everything to the same few CPUs while others idle; the balancer can't fix a mask you set.
- Pinning two hot threads to SMT siblings, so they compete for one core.
- Hard-coded CPU numbers that are wrong on the next machine, or inside a container that was given different CPUs.

## Key takeaways
- Scheduling domains represent hardware locality and guide balancing.
- The scheduler balances periodically, before idling and when placing waking tasks.
- Hard affinity and cpusets limit the balancer’s choices; validate CPU numbers and measure the result.

## Further reading
- [Multiprocessor Scheduling (Advanced) — OSTEP](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/cpu-sched-multi.pdf)
- [Scheduler Domains — Linux kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-domains.html)
- [CFS Bandwidth Control — Linux kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-bwc.html)
- [Control Group v2 — Linux kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html)
- [sched_setaffinity(2) — Linux manual page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/sched_setaffinity.2.html)
- [numa(7) — Linux manual page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/numa.7.html)
- [Non-uniform memory access — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-uniform_memory_access)


That would be the union. sched_setaffinity sets a new mask rather than adding to the old one.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Linux's multicore CPU load balancing are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: A CPU that is about to go idle tries to pull work from a busier CPU first
options.explanation: Correct. This is 'newidle' balancing, one of the three triggers alongside periodic and wake-up balancing.

options.text: Balancing across NUMA nodes is done as eagerly as between SMT siblings
options.explanation: It's the reverse. Moving between siblings is cheap (shared caches), so it happens readily; crossing NUMA nodes loses cache and memory locality, so it's done reluctantly.

options.text: When a thread wakes, the kernel prefers its previous CPU or an idle CPU sharing the same last-level cache
options.explanation: Correct. Wake-up placement balances keeping a warm cache against finding an idle CPU quickly.

options.text: A task that ran very recently may be treated as cache-hot and left where it is
options.explanation: Correct. Below the migration-cost threshold (0.5 ms by default) the balancer prefers not to move it.

options.text: Load is measured purely as the number of runnable tasks on each CPU
options.explanation: Linux considers runnable counts alongside PELT load, runnable and utilization averages, CPU capacity and other signals. It does not rely purely on task counts.

questions.workedExample: The correct statements are A, C and D. Newidle balancing may pull work; wake-up placement considers locality and idle CPUs; recently running tasks may be treated as cache-hot. Cross-node balancing has different costs. Linux uses multiple signals, including task counts and distinct PELT averages; no one metric describes every balancing decision.

lessons.title: Place memory near the threads that use it
lessons.summary: New private anonymous pages commonly follow the first write under local policy, subject to allocation and migration rules.
lessons.body:
## NUMA: memory has an address *and* a location

On a multi-socket server, each node's memory is local to its cores. Remote memory access cost and interconnect bandwidth depend on the machine and workload.

> [!note] Content gap
> No reproducible machine-specific NUMA measurements accompany this lesson, so no universal remote/local latency multiplier is provided. `numactl --hardware` shows the nodes and a distance table (10 means local; remote nodes are larger, commonly around 20).

Linux normally prefers local allocation. For new private anonymous memory, the first write fault commonly allocates a page near the executing CPU. Explicit policies, cpusets, fallback under memory pressure, huge pages and later migration can change placement. That causes a classic bug:

> [!example] The single-threaded initialiser
> A program allocates and zeroes a 64 GiB array in its main thread on node 0, then starts 32 worker threads spread across both nodes. Assume the main thread stays on node 0, local memory is sufficient, writes fault in new pages and no policy or migration changes placement. The pages then start on node 0. Half the workers make every access remotely, and node 0's memory bandwidth is shared by everyone. Fix: initialise each slice from the thread that will use it, or interleave.

Tools and policies:

- `numactl --cpunodebind=0 --membind=0 ./db` runs a process on node 0's CPUs with node 0's memory.
- `numactl --interleave=all` spreads pages round robin across nodes: distributed allocation rather than guaranteed per-thread locality. It can reduce concentration on one node, but does not guarantee removal of all hot spots. Often a good choice for large shared caches, such as a database buffer pool.
- **Automatic NUMA balancing** (since Linux 3.8, `kernel.numa_balancing`): the kernel periodically unmaps pages to sample which node touches them through "hinting faults", then migrates pages towards their users, or tasks towards their memory. It helps long-running, well-partitioned workloads, at the cost of some overhead.
- `numastat -p <pid>` shows where a process's memory actually lives.

The scheduler is NUMA-aware: its top-level scheduling domain balances reluctantly across nodes, because moving a thread can turn accesses to its existing memory into remote accesses; cache hits and pages already elsewhere are exceptions.

## Key takeaways
- New private anonymous pages commonly follow the first write under local policy, subject to allocation and migration rules.
- Initialising each worker’s slice can preserve locality; interleaving distributes allocation instead.
- Remote/local cost depends on hardware and workload; use NUMA tools rather than a universal multiplier.

questions.prompt: A main thread pinned to NUMA node 0 writes every page of a new private 100 GiB array, with enough local memory and no explicit policy or migration. Workers then run on both nodes and bandwidth falls below expectations. Which placement problem fits this setup?

options.text: The workers are being throttled by a cgroup quota
options.explanation: Nothing in the scenario mentions a CPU limit. The clue is who touched the memory first.

options.text: The array is too large for the L3 cache
options.explanation: True of any 100 GiB array, but it doesn't explain why this layout is slow compared with alternatives.

options.text: Linux allocates huge arrays across both nodes evenly by default
options.explanation: The default is first touch, not page interleaving. That's exactly why the layout is lopsided.

options.text: First-touch placed the pages on node 0, concentrating memory traffic there; workers on the other node need remote service for misses to those pages
options.explanation: Correct. Initialise each slice from the thread that will use it, interleave pages with `numactl --interleave`, or let automatic NUMA balancing migrate pages over time.

questions.workedExample: Under the stated assumptions, first-write faults allocate the new pages on node 0. Workers on node 1 then need remote memory for cache misses to those pages, and requests concentrate on node 0. The exact cost is hardware-dependent; no measured multiplier is available here. Parallel initialization, deliberate page interleaving or matching workers to memory can improve placement, subject to measurement.

lessons.title: Separate CPU shares from CPU quota
lessons.summary: Weight sets relative shares only when groups compete.
lessons.body:
## Containers: shares versus quotas

Containers use cgroups to control CPU in two very different ways.

| Control | cgroup v2 file | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| Weight | `cpu.weight` | Share *under contention* |
| Quota | `cpu.max` | Hard cap, even when idle CPUs exist |

**Weight** (default 100) is proportional sharing between groups, just like nice between threads. If the machine is otherwise idle, a low-weight container can still use every CPU. It's *work-conserving*.

A **CPU quota** is set through CFS bandwidth control. `cpu.max` holds two numbers, "quota period", in microseconds. Dividing one by the other tells you how many CPUs' worth of time the group may use:

```formula
N_eff = Q / P
N_eff = 200000 µs / 100000 µs = 2
where
N_eff: the group's quota-to-period capacity ceiling in CPUs' worth of service; it can be fractional and is not an affinity mask
Q: the quota, the CPU time the whole group may use in each period, in microseconds (µs); 200000 µs = 200 ms here
P: the period, the length of each accounting window, in µs; 100000 µs = 100 ms here
µs: microseconds, millionths of a second
In words: 200 ms of CPU time in every 100 ms window is the same as keeping two CPUs fully busy.
```

So `200000 100000` means 200 ms of CPU time per 100 ms period, 2 CPUs' worth. Fair-class CPU time is charged across the group. Exhausted local bandwidth allocations cause throttling even with idle CPUs. Ancestor quotas, per-CPU runtime accounting and configured burst credit also affect the exact timeline.

In Kubernetes, a pod's CPU **request** becomes its cgroup weight, and its CPU **limit** becomes its `cpu.max` quota (with the default 100 ms period).

## Key takeaways
- Weight sets relative shares only when groups compete.
- Quota limits aggregate CPU time per period, even when unused host CPUs exist.
- The quota-to-period ratio expresses a capacity ceiling; ancestor limits and accounting details also apply.

## Further reading
- [Multiprocessor Scheduling (Advanced) — OSTEP](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/cpu-sched-multi.pdf)
- [Scheduler Domains — Linux kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-domains.html)
- [CFS Bandwidth Control — Linux kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-bwc.html)
- [Control Group v2 — Linux kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html)
- [sched_setaffinity(2) — Linux manual page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/sched_setaffinity.2.html)
- [numa(7) — Linux manual page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/numa.7.html)
- [Non-uniform memory access — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-uniform_memory_access)
- [Go 1.25 release notes (container-aware GOMAXPROCS)](https://go.dev/doc/go1.25)

questions.prompt: A fair-class batch container has cpu.weight=10, no leaf or ancestor quota, access to all 16 physical cores, and enough runnable workers. With no competing work, how much CPU can it use?

options.text: All 16 cores
options.explanation: Correct. Weight only matters under contention. With no competitors, the low-weight group gets everything: weights are work-conserving.

options.text: About 10% of one core
options.explanation: That treats weight as a hard cap. Caps come from cpu.max; weight is a relative share.

options.text: About 1.6 cores (10% of 16)
options.explanation: Again a cap interpretation. Weight 10 means 'a tenth as much as a weight-100 group when both want CPU', not 10% of the machine.

options.text: None until a weight-100 group gives up the CPU
options.explanation: There are no other groups, and weights never stop a group from using idle CPUs.

questions.workedExample:
1. `cpu.weight` is proportional sharing between groups that are **competing**.
2. Here no other group wants CPU, so its share of the contended CPU is 10 / 10 = 100%.
3. With 16 cores and enough threads, it can use all 16.

If a weight-100 group then became busy, each group's share would be its weight over the total:

```formula
s = w / (w + w_other)
s = 10 / (10 + 100) ≈ 0.09
where
s: the batch container's share of the CPU while both groups are busy
w: its cpu.weight, 10
w_other: the competing group's cpu.weight, 100
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: under contention it gets about 9 % and the other group about 91 %.
```

A hard ceiling would need `cpu.max`.

lessons.title: Trace throttling and its effect on request latency
lessons.summary: Several runnable threads can consume an aggregate CPU budget before the period ends.
lessons.body:
## How throttling wrecks tail latency

**Worked example: two CPUs of quota, eight busy threads.** A container has `cpu.max = 200000 100000` and a server with 8 worker threads, on a 32-core host. In an idealised model, all 8 run simultaneously from the period boundary, with no other contention, overhead, burst credit or carried local runtime. Eight threads on eight CPUs burn 8 ms of CPU time for every millisecond of wall-clock time, so:

```formula
t_run = Q / n = 200 ms / 8 = 25 ms
t_thr = P − t_run = 100 ms − 25 ms
t_thr = 75 ms
t_lat = (P − t_a) + t_cpu
t_lat = (100 − 26) ms + 5 ms = 79 ms
where
t_run: how long into each period the quota lasts, in milliseconds (ms)
Q: the quota per period, 200 ms of CPU time
n: the number of threads running at once, 8
t_thr: how long the whole container is throttled (stopped) for in each period, in ms
P: the period, 100 ms
t_lat: the latency of a request that arrives while the container is throttled, in ms
t_a: when the request arrives, measured from the start of the period: 26 ms here
t_cpu: the CPU time the request needs, 5 ms here
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
In words: eight threads use up a two-CPU budget in a quarter of the period, then everything stops for the other three quarters, and a request that arrives during the stop waits for the next period.
```

So for the remaining **75 ms** of each period nothing in the container runs, and a request arriving 26 ms into the period has a latency of at least 79 ms; queueing behind existing work can add more. Average usage is "2 CPUs, within limit", so dashboards look fine.

The symptom is p99 latency far above p50 while CPU usage looks modest. Check `cpu.stat`:

```
nr_periods 36000
nr_throttled 9100
throttled_usec 412000000
```

The fraction of periods that ended in throttling is one counter divided by the other:

```formula
f_thr = nr_throttled / nr_periods
f_thr = 9100 / 36000 ≈ 0.25
where
f_thr: the fraction of enforcement periods in which the group ran out of quota
nr_throttled: the number of periods in which the group was throttled
nr_periods: the number of periods in which the group had runnable work
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: about one period in four ended with the group out of quota.
```

Here a quarter of periods were throttled. Ways out:

- **Size thread pools to the quota, not the host.** Eight threads chewing through two CPUs' quota in a quarter of the period is worse than two threads using it smoothly.
- **Remove CPU limits** for latency-sensitive services and rely on requests (weights) for fairness. The trade-off is weaker isolation from competing workloads; inherited parent quotas can still throttle the group.
- **Allow bursting**: `cpu.max.burst` (Linux 5.14+) lets a group bank unused quota for short spikes.
- **Use exclusive CPUs** (eligible Guaranteed containers under Kubernetes static CPU management; whole cores require appropriate policy options) when you need both isolation and predictability.

## Key takeaways
- Several runnable threads can consume an aggregate CPU budget before the period ends.
- Requests arriving during throttling wait for service to resume and may also queue behind other work.
- Compare throttled periods with enforcement periods and test concurrency, quotas and isolation changes.

## Further reading
- [Multiprocessor Scheduling (Advanced) — OSTEP](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/cpu-sched-multi.pdf)
- [Scheduler Domains — Linux kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-domains.html)
- [CFS Bandwidth Control — Linux kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-bwc.html)
- [Control Group v2 — Linux kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html)
- [sched_setaffinity(2) — Linux manual page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/sched_setaffinity.2.html)
- [numa(7) — Linux manual page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/numa.7.html)
- [Non-uniform memory access — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-uniform_memory_access)
- [Go 1.25 release notes (container-aware GOMAXPROCS)](https://go.dev/doc/go1.25)

questions.prompt: In an idealized quota model, a container has cpu.max = 300000 100000. Ten threads run continuously on ten CPUs from each period boundary, without contention, overhead, burst credit or carried runtime. How long is the group throttled in each 100 ms period?

options.text: 0 ms; 3 CPUs of quota is plenty on a 32-core host
options.explanation: The quota is shared by all threads across all CPUs. Ten busy threads burn through it faster than three would.

options.text: 70 ms
options.explanation: Correct. 10 threads consume 10 CPU-ms per ms, so 300 ms of quota lasts 30 ms. The remaining 70 ms is throttled.

options.text: 30 ms
options.explanation: That's how long the container *runs* before the quota is exhausted, not how long it is throttled.

options.text: 97 ms
options.explanation: That assumes each thread is limited to 0.3 ms. The quota is a pooled budget, not a per-thread one.

questions.workedExample:
1. Quota: 300 ms of CPU per 100 ms period (3 CPUs' worth).
2. Ten busy threads use 10 ms of CPU time for every millisecond of wall-clock time.

```formula
t_run = Q / n = 300 ms / 10 = 30 ms
t_thr = P − t_run
t_thr = 100 ms − 30 ms = 70 ms
where
t_run: how long the quota lasts in each period, in milliseconds (ms)
Q: the quota, 300 ms of CPU time per period
n: the number of threads running at once, 10
t_thr: how long the group is throttled in each period, in ms
P: the period, 100 ms
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
In words: ten threads spend a three-CPU budget in 30 ms, then wait 70 ms for the next period.
```

Average use is 3 CPUs, exactly the limit, so a dashboard looks healthy. But any request arriving during those 70 ms waits until the period ends. That's the tail-latency trap.

questions.prompt: A latency-sensitive service in a container shows p99 far above p50 and `nr_throttled` rising fast, while average CPU is below its limit. Which changes are likely to help? Select all that apply.

options.text: Shrink the worker pool to roughly the CPU quota
options.explanation: Correct. Fewer threads consume the quota more smoothly, so it lasts the whole period instead of being exhausted early.

options.text: Remove the CPU limit and rely on the CPU request (weight) for fairness
options.explanation: Correct, if no ancestor quota remains: removing the limiting bandwidth cap can remove this cause of throttling. Fairness then depends on competing weights and available CPUs.

options.text: Allow bursting with cpu.max.burst
options.explanation: Accumulated unused burst credit can absorb a short spike. It does not create unlimited CPU capacity, and sustained overload or absent credit can still throttle.

options.text: Raise the pod's cpu.weight (CPU request) but keep the same limit
options.explanation: Raising weight does not raise the hard quota. It can change competition and the timing of budget consumption, but does not remove the bandwidth cap.

options.text: Add more worker threads so requests don't queue
options.explanation: More threads burn the quota faster and make throttling worse.

questions.workedExample: A smaller CPU-bound pool can consume budget more smoothly; removing all relevant quota caps avoids quota throttling; accumulated burst credit can absorb short spikes. Raising weight does not raise the quota. More workers can exhaust it earlier. These are workload-dependent remedies: compare throughput and latency, and inspect ancestor limits.

questions.prompt: A container's `cpu.stat` over the last hour shows `nr_periods 36000` and `nr_throttled 14400`, with the default 100 ms period. What does this tell you?

options.text: The container was throttled for 14,400 seconds
options.explanation: nr_throttled counts periods in which throttling happened, not seconds. The time is in throttled_usec.

options.text: Throttling was reported for 40% of the counted periods; request latency needs separate measurement
options.explanation: Correct. 14400 / 36000 = 0.4. Two periods in five ended with the group out of quota.

options.text: It used 40% of its quota on average
options.explanation: nr_throttled doesn't measure average usage. A group can be throttled often while averaging well under its quota.

options.text: Nothing; nr_throttled only counts throttling of real-time tasks
options.explanation: These cpu.stat fields come from CFS bandwidth control, which applies to normal tasks.

questions.workedExample:
```formula
f_thr = nr_throttled / nr_periods
f_thr = 14400 / 36000 = 0.4 = 40 %
T = 36000 × 100 ms = 3600 s
where
f_thr: the fraction of counted periods in which throttling happened
nr_throttled: periods with throttling, 14400
nr_periods: enforcement periods with runnable work, 36000
T: the wall-clock time those periods cover if they ran back to back, in seconds (s): one hour
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
s: seconds
%: per cent, hundredths
In words: two periods in every five ended with the group out of quota.
```

These counters alone do not measure request latency or the fraction of wall time stalled. Compare interval deltas, throttled_usec, usage and latency measurements; throttled time can aggregate across per-CPU run queues.

questions.prompt: In an idealized quota model, cpu.max = 50000 100000. One request needs 80 ms CPU and starts at a period boundary. Assume no other work, contention, overhead, burst credit or carried runtime. Roughly when does it finish?

options.text: At 80 ms
options.explanation: That ignores the quota. Only 50 ms of CPU is allowed per 100 ms period.

options.text: At 160 ms
options.explanation: That spreads the work evenly at half speed. Bandwidth control doesn't slow a thread down; it lets it run at full speed, then stops it.

options.text: At about 130 ms
options.explanation: Correct. It runs 0–50 ms, is throttled 50–100 ms, then runs its remaining 30 ms from 100 to 130 ms.

options.text: At 200 ms
options.explanation: The second period doesn't need to be used in full; the request finishes 30 ms into it.

questions.workedExample:
Walk the periods:

```
0    50   100  130
|run |thr |run|
 50ms  -    30ms
```

1. Period 1 (0–100): runs 50 ms, quota gone at 50, throttled until 100.
2. Period 2 (100–200): needs 30 more ms; runs 100–130 and finishes.

```formula
t_end = P + (C − Q)
t_end = 100 ms + (80 ms − 50 ms)
t_end = 130 ms
where
t_end: when the request finishes, measured from the start of the first period, in milliseconds (ms)
P: the period, 100 ms
C: the CPU time the request needs, 80 ms
Q: the quota per period, 50 ms
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
In words: it gets 50 ms in the first period, waits for the second, and needs 30 ms more once it starts.
```

So 80 ms of CPU takes about 130 ms of wall time. A request arriving just after the quota ran out would fare worse: it would wait up to 50 ms before starting.

lessons.title: Count usable CPU capacity inside containers
lessons.summary: Visible host CPU count, affinity and cgroup quota describe different limits.
lessons.body:
## Runtimes that count the wrong CPUs

Many runtimes size their worker pools from the CPU count, and the CPU count visible inside a container is usually the **host's**:

- Python's `os.cpu_count()` returns the host's logical CPUs. `os.process_cpu_count()` (3.13+) respects the affinity mask, but **not** a `cpu.max` quota.
- Go 1.25 introduced container-aware defaults: logical CPUs, affinity and cgroup CPU bandwidth all participate. Fractional quotas are rounded up, and the default generally stays at least 2 unless CPU count or affinity is lower. Explicit settings and compatibility controls can override this.
- The JVM has been container-aware since JDK 10 (backported to 8u191).

For example, 64 visible logical CPUs, no narrower affinity and no Python CPU-count override can yield a default maximum of 64 processes despite a two-CPU quota. Workers start as jobs are submitted, with behavior depending on Python version and start method. A simple cgroup-v2 quota reader is:

```python
PATH = "/sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max"

def cpu_quota():
    try:
        # Read one visible budget pair.
        with open(PATH) as f:
            quota, period = f.read().split()
    except FileNotFoundError:
        return None  # not cgroup v2
    if quota == "max":
        return None  # no limit
    # CPU-time budget per unit wall time.
    return int(quota) / int(period)

# "200000 100000" -> 2.0
# Assumes this path is the relevant cgroup.
```

This helper reads one visible cgroup only. It does not discover the process's cgroup or ancestor limits, handle cgroup v1, or combine quota with affinity. An unlimited leaf can still have a constrained ancestor.
## Pitfalls

- **Treating CPU limits as harmless.** A quota caps every period, not the average. Bursty, multi-threaded services get throttled while looking underused.
- **Ignoring SMT.** "16 CPUs" may be 8 cores. Two hot threads on siblings don't double throughput.
- **Over-pinning.** A hard affinity mask disables the balancer's ability to help; it's only better when you've measured.
- **NUMA-blind initialisation.** First touch puts memory where it's first written, not where it's used.
- **Trusting `cpu_count()`** inside containers.

## Key takeaways
- Visible host CPU count, affinity and cgroup quota describe different limits.
- Runtime defaults depend on versions and configuration; verify what the deployed interpreter uses.
- A single cpu.max reader is illustrative and does not discover ancestor limits or combine all constraints.

## Further reading

- [Scheduler Domains — Linux kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/scheduler/sched-domains.html)

questions.prompt: On Linux Python 3.13+, with 64 visible logical CPUs, no CPU-count override or affinity restriction, a pod has a two-CPU quota. A default ProcessPoolExecutor is given enough CPU-bound jobs to fill it. What problem can occur?

options.text: It starts 2 workers, because Python reads the cgroup quota
options.explanation: `os.cpu_count()` (and `process_cpu_count()`) don't read cpu.max. Python doesn't see the quota.

options.text: Up to 64 workers compete for two CPUs of aggregate quota, risking heavy throttling
options.explanation: Correct. The default maximum uses process_cpu_count(), which considers affinity but not CPU bandwidth quota. Running many CPU-bound workers can exhaust each period budget early.

options.text: It starts 64 workers, and the limit stops being enforced because there are more processes than CPUs
options.explanation: The quota applies to all processes in the cgroup, however many there are.

options.text: It fails to start because 64 exceeds the limit
options.explanation: Nothing checks pool size against the quota. The workers start; they just can't all run.

questions.workedExample: With the specified environment, process_cpu_count() returns 64, so the default maximum is 64 workers. Their CPU time shares the two-CPU quota. Enough runnable workers may exhaust the budget early and then wait for replenishment. Benchmark a smaller pool; discover effective affinity and cgroup hierarchy limits rather than assuming the host count is usable bandwidth.
